The true combination of the tasty and nu- tritious is ideal cookery. Bovril is popular in the kitchen for the ease and. celerity with which various dishes can be made by its aid; its deli- cious flavour and its singular nourishing power are well known. It makes a delicate and strengthening soup and a good gravy. It gives a delicious flavour to ragouts, croquettes,rissoles and all entrees. It is so direct and unfailing in its nutritive effects on the system, and of so at- tractive a flavour, that it is suited alike to the epicure, the athlete, and the invalid. It is the very embodiment of sustenance. No cook who aims at culinary successes at a small cost and at a short notice, can do without Bovril.

Bovril is prepared from cattle raised on the richest pasture lands of the world. The pro- cesses of manufacture, conducted under the supervision of skilled analysts, ensure the reten- tion in the most easily digested form, of all the nourishing, stimulating, vitalising principles of the primest ox beef, whereas ordinary meat ex- tracts meiely stimulate without nourishing.

Bovril increases vitality; makes the weak strong, and the strong stronger. For invalids and convalescents it is simply perfect, because it is an easily assimilatecl,sustaining,strengthen- ing food, which can be relished and retained when other foods, liciid or solid, are either rejected or impossible.

The Government ara deliberating on the desira- bility of introducing a Bill next session to amend and extend the Workmen's Compensation Act. Some of its provisions have been pretty well riddled al- ready by judicial decisions and judicial comments, and the amount of litigation it has given rise to I must have rather disturbed the optimism of Mr. Chamberlain and of thy:, Home Secretary. If the Government were not themselves to take the 1 amendment of the Act in hand, a private member's i Bill would be brought in, which they could • not I refuse to adopt, and they may, therefore, as well take the credit of making their own legislative structure as perfect as they can. It is obvious that they will be pre:sed also to extend the Act to some of the excluded trades, and they may as well likewise take the credit of extend- ' lug it on their own initiative, which they are, I be- 1 lieve, inclined to do. It is certainly difficult to see how they can avoid amending the Act so as to pre- vent it from being swamped by litigation, and by decisions adverse to the repeated iitclarations of Ministers of their intentions during its passage through Parliament. Sandhurst will shortly send another batch of cadets into the army, but the instalment will be ab- sorbed without making any appreciable difference in the deficiency of junior officers in either the cavalry or the infantry. The position of the army in this respect is without parallel in recent years. At no time sincl the introduction of the competi- tive system has entrance to the commiesioned rank been easier. To such an extent has the standard of oualification been relaxed that the profession is really open at the present moment to any educated youth of suitable age. Still, the door will have to be opened furthPr it the deficiency of officers is to be made up. There are candidates in abundance, but even if a new Code were adopt el it would necessarily take a year or two before the old balance could be adjusted. During the past year the num- ber of secondinge has increased by 20 per cent, and most of the infantry battalions are now short by several lieutenants. The state of the cavalry is even worse,in spite of the long list of first appointments in last week's "Gazette." One cavalry regiment at least is entirely without second lieutenants. No doubt the Horse Guards' Staff are to blame for not having foreseen the extent to which the service Iwas certain to be depleted by the recent extension of extra-regimental emp:t.oyment.

London has had a fair share of Christmas eensa- tions,e.nd tee riverside suburb or village of Barking, with its Daystedotas case of child-murder and its yet unexelained boiler explosion,has had more than enough. It appears ae if the bearaess murder of %le little girl will add another to the somewhat long list of crimes the Loadon police have been un- able to trace to their authors. The act is rather that of a lunatic, or some pereon not cognisant of the nature of his actions, than of a mere callous hu- man brute. At the same time, the latter class of mortals are common enough in the annals of crime. The greater horror of the explo+ion seems likely also to remain a mystery. No official theory as to its cause is forthcoming. From all that is known there is nothing to show that if the victims of the explosion had been spared they could have thrown any light on the ceetee of it. It may be that the gauge was eat of order, and experts may be able to say whether the recorded pressure of 15lbs.to the square inch could have effeeted such tremendous ,results. This shocking calamity will surely lead to - a more effective application of the Boiler Explosions Act. A metropolitan Board of Guardians is trying an experiment which may have been attempted else- where but which is new to London. It has been found difficult, hitherto, to obtain situations for young mate inmates unless their sustenance is pro- vided for. As a kind of half-way house between the workhouse and, perfect freedom, the board of guardians referred t 3 has leased a house for the accommodation of lads who go out to work. They will still be under discipline and supervision, with, however, a much larger amount of freedom than if they coatinued to live in the workhouse. This departure is so clearly backed by common sense that the example is sure to be followed. The tablet which,as I mentioned some weeks ago, is to be fixed upon one of the wall-piers of Sir Reginald Palgrave's official residence in New Palace Yard to indicate the eite of the old Stier Chamber, is now in the hands of the Office of Works Superin- tendent, and will be placed in position forthwith. The inscription runs as follows :—" This tablet marks the position of the outer doorway leading to the room, built during the year 1602, wherein the Court of Law constituted by Statute 3, Hen. VII., C. 1, known as the Star Chamber Court,held session -during the reign of James I. and Charles I. until August 1, 1641, when the Court was closed by Statute 16, Car. 1, C. 10. The position of the door- way was astertained by measurements based upon ancient plans of the Palace of Westminster. The frontage of the Star Chamber building extended about thirty feet northward and southward from this spot. The Star Chamber was upon the first thole and wae lighted by windows looking towards Isew Palace Yard." The wall-pier upon which the tablet is to be placed is situated midway between the two archways which give access irom New Palace Yard to the Speaker's Court. Thanks te Sir Edward Clarke's timely, if spiteful letter, the highly-ornamental committee of the Gladstone-National Memorial is at length awaken- ing.from its letharoy. Hitherto the committee has suffered from the disadvantage of being too un- wieldy tor ectien. Nioreover, the extremely aris- tocratic character of its composition has preyed a mixed blessing. Most of the members bear such in- fluential names that there had been a tendency to rely on their magnetic power alone. There WaB good reason, of course, for making the committee beth liege and Influential. The object PM to em- phasiee the national and non-partisan espect of the scheme, and this could not be better dene than by getting men like the Duke of Rutland, the-Duke ef Argyll, and the mew Viceroy of India to lend their names. A committee within the committee has now pot to work,and within a few days public meetings zsell be organized in different parts of the country. Literature will be distributed and local officials ap- pointed to receive subscriptions. It is stated, too that since the publication of Sir B. Clarke's letter the flow of subscriptions to the central fund has received a decided stimulus. Altogether the fund would seem to have bad few more valuable_contri-

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY Dun NELLIE,

I commence my letter this week with a reference to evening dresses. This is a description of a dress which I saw the other day. It had a black skirt, trimmed at the hem with tiny flounces, and with it was worn a décolleté, guipure bodice. A fichu chemisette of gaze de soie framed the bodice, which is encircled at the waist by a black velvet band. The gaze de soie black or white. The guipure bodice is charming • it is sometimes suc- cessfully made in black tulle embroidered in jet, with large flowers. Another combination adapting itself more successfully to a close-fitting gown of plush or muslin velvet is a very deep flounce of guipure over the material at the base of the skirt. Liberty satin forming the skirt has the guipure resting on a thick ruche. The décolleté bodice, cut round, fits closely, and was fastened under the arm, and finished off with a ruffle of guipure at the throat, attached to the shoulders by tufts of flowers or knots of gaze de soie, instead of sleeves. The incrustation of guipure can be equally well supported by a foundation of crepe de chine in Sevre blue or vieux rose. The bodice will then be gathered beneath a short bodice of guipure. The skirt will be trimmed with detached flowers or a pointed insertion, shaped as a peplum and touching the hem at intervals.

There seems to be no end to the stylish novel- ties in millinery which are now being shown in the leading modistes' windows, and it is really astonishing that so many models should be pro- duced in distinctive styles. I saw a delightful hat recently. It was really a toque, but it appeared to be so hidden in trimming that it was almost impossible to obtain/a view of the shape of the toque er even of the toque itself. It was trimmed with black net, edged with fur of an intense blackness. There were, too, large feathers on the left side of the hat, and behind them was placed others feathers in black and white. Perhaps I might more correctly describe them as tips. The hair of a person who fitted it, and who it suited immensely had no fringe, but her hair was combed back loosely, and I should say that it would be likely to suit such a person.

A fashion that is rapidly coming in is welcome to many ladies because it provides them with an outer garment most suitable for walking on fine days, and quite elaborate enough for the indoor func- tions that enliven winter afternoons. These are the rich black peau-de-soie or brocade coats with warm quilted linings, which are trimmed with really fine black passementerie, or embroidered with black silk and cut jet beads, which are very different from the common, heavy moulded beads that distinguish cheap trimmings. Black silk coats, however, are, never seen without some kind of white relief in front, such as white satin revers veiled with guipure, or large bows, jabots, or waterfalls of good lace, the latter being naturally the most truly economical. The coat may also be edged with black fur around the top of the collar.

Few people know the great value of saffron spies as a valuable addition to diet in cases of nervous disorders, neuralgia, dyspepsia, and like ailments. The best mode of administering it is in milk food, such as ,rice, sago, bread, semolina, cornflower, and other milk pudding,. For this purpose the saffron should be tied in a small piece of Brussels net or fine muslin, and boiled in the milk. Care should be taken to procure the saffron of good quality, and nob previously used for extract purposes' as much of what is sold has been. It can also be used in beef and chicken broth, aud in Germany no bouillon is made without it. A good many friends of your acquaintance will require pretty dresses during the festive season for family and friendly dinner parties, for evening gatherings that are not exactly balls, though there may be a little carpet dancing, and for the visits to the theatre that always come off at such seasons. A friend was wearing a very nice dinner gown in white satin, embroidered with jet, and with black lace flounces, epaulettea and frills to the chiffon elbow sleeves. On each side of the moderately low-cut bodice there was a small cluster of yellow poppies, with three rows of large iridescent beads festooned between them. Another had a very pretty style Of dinner dress in white or black satin and chiffon, with a white lace skirt. The fanciful cut corsage was bordered with purple velvet. The special feature, however, was the novel style of frilled white chiffon fichu laid round the decolletage and secured with Parisian diamond clasps at irregular intervals. They will, I am sure, not be annoyed if you copy them.
Yonr loving
;TENNIS.

div.head: [HE EXAMINER FRIDAY, JANUARY 13 1899
div.p: [HE EXAMINER FRIDAY, JANUARY 13 1899
"WOMEN'S CHAT.

The appointment of Sir James Reid, who succeeds Sir William Jenner, as Physician-in-Chief to Her Majesty, recalls to mind the fact that during the whole of her reign, the Queen blur consulted only three physicians. Sir James Clark had charge of the Sovereign for the first 25 years, for the next 27 years Sir William denner under- took the responsibility, from which Sir James Reid re- lieved him, nine years ago. The post of Resident Medical Attendant is by no means the sinecure it is supposed to be, as it necessitates close personal attenoance on Her Majesty. According to preeent arrangements,Princess Christian will hold the February Drawing Rooms tcr the Queen, the Princess of Wales being unable to represent Her Majesty, on account of her deep mourning. The state- ment to the effect that.the Duchess of York will hold one of the Drawing Rooms this coming season for the Queen has no foundation in fact. It would be impossible for the Duchess to represent Her Majesty at such a fuection as the Queen's daughters have precedence durini her lifetime. There will be but one Royal debutante this year—bonde Princess Margaret of Connaught. At a Drawing Room held by the Queen herself, there is always a faint hope cherished by those attenoing it, that the Sovereign may possibly remaie in the Throne Room for a little while, after those have passed who possess the privilege of the entree. Anyone who has witnessed the tremendous rush on the staircase, and at the barriers, can estimate at its true value,the prevalent desire to appear bsfore Rer Majesty. I have seen a mass of struggling wornee, their long veils catching in aeh others jewels, the feathers on their trains crushed and flattened, and their toquets suffering much from the rush and crowd. Those who are most intent on being first, seem to feel the greatest amount of annoyance about the strenuous efforts of others to the same end. Cloaks aud mantles, some of them extremely sumptuous are left in the Hew Library, before their owners ascend the stairs, and sometimes they are merely flung down, so great is the haste to be in good time at the Throne Room. Speaking of bcquets, when one recalls the fashionable specimen of say twenty years back, with every sort of flower massed closely together, the blossoms pressed so tightly stalk to stalk as to make them fade and wither in a very short space of time, sled the whole surrounded with an ornamental paper,one can but be thankful that this state of affairs obtains no longer. The exquisite art which now concerns itself with the light wed grace- ful disposition of the lovely flowers to be seen at every Draw Mg Room is unsurpassable. In nothing more than the arrangement of flowers and boquets, has the im- proved taste ot the age, been exhib;ted of late. The Empress Frederick, during her brief stay in Lon- don, on the conclusion of her visit to the Queen, spent a busy time, accomplishing an almost increoible amount of work, which she bad set herself to do. Her Majesty's visit to these shores has Ldeed been a lengthened (me— extending over four months. The next few weeks will be sr eat in Italy. at the Hotel Angst, kierdighera, where elaborate preparations have ben made for her reception. 'this will be the first time that the Empress ban visited Riviera since the last illness of her husband, when the Imperial pair resided at the Villa Lurio, at Sam Remo, from November 3rd, 1887 to March 10th 1888 The Em- press. when German Crown Princess, as very fond of the Eastern Riviera, and she then r aid frequent visits to Pee to Fino. Santa Margarita de Lavante, and other places on the coast between Genoa and Spezzia. Influenza has been attacking many persons in high place of late. Among the vic,ims may be mentioned the German Emperor, Prince Max, of Saxony, the Grand Duke Paul of Russia, the Queen of the Be glans, and her youngest daughter. the Princess Clementine. The latter will be obliged to spend the next three or four months on the Riviera. Among less exalted folk, ir- fluenza has been busy too, and we should a.l do well, at this most trying seesen of the year, to avoid chills and colds, which render us such easy prey to the dread enemy. It i quite possible to be very wall dressed, and yefr' very ill clothed. In evening attire, this is, of course, conspicuously true, but I refer to outdoor garments. During the east windy days that fell to our lot recently, there was no lack of instances of the kind. Girls en bicycles were riding without ccats, women in short capes shivered with co'd, though these capcs consisted ef the very warmest furs and fabrics known to civilisa- tion. The arms were unprotected by teem save on the shoulders, and the lower part of the lungs felt the cold all the more for the exceeding warmth of the covering on the upper portion. I noticed a woman taking her walk abroad one morning, magnificently attired, but miserably clothed. Her skirt was co h, wi h a band of sable round the hem. She wore a sable bolero,ft sleeve- less shing, which opened in front, and left the chest ex- posed to the keen and biter blast A cascade of very pretty lace did what it could to supply the ornission,but ' needless to say, it was little use. Some few of our countrywomen manage to combine smartness with efficsent shelter against the climate, but the majority either overshoot, or fall short cf the) mark. Enormously heavy cloaks are worn by the first contin- gent in walking costume, fur trimmed and elabcrately lined, absolutely imp-netrable to the air, and as opposed to neceseary ventilatiou, as the ancient mode of water- proof—and so happily surereeded by the process of cravenetting. The re suit of heaping on warm cicthes is usually to achieve the opposite of the desired re tit; and to facilitate the catching of colds. Mountains of cloth- ing are mistakes, quite as much as inadequate quanti- ties. That faulty piece of philosophy " Keep a thing seven years, and you are sure to find use for it should be amenced, and some longer period fiecr d doring which to keep that which cur discernment warns us is worthy to treasure. Take for example the lone ostrich feather, that appears once more on all up-to-date headgear. 1 cannot remember the exact year in which it last poised itself round the hat of the period, but lam ready to assert it is nearer seventeen than seven year ago: But what to keep is the matter for fine discrimination. How to distinguish between the thing of passing value, and that of permanent. Perhaps featbers, furs and lace, are almost the only items of which one may be absolutely certain that they should be stowed away. About the keeping of gowns, these are hardly two opinions in the minds of the sensible. For holding the blouse and skirt together, safety pins are usecren evidence especially the new double safety pins made with a heok on one, and an eye on the other. These hocks and eyes are occasionally very elaborate. Sometime- they may be seen in diamonds, cr other precions stones, when they do double duty, being highly ornamental, and very useful, at one and the same time. Violet in all shades, frcm the palest mauve to the deeps at purple, is well to the fore at the moment. In- deed many of the most successful cloth gowns for the winter are carried out in two shades of violet. A delight- ful frock, I raw at a leading modistes last week, was of dark violet cloth,the strapping. b-ing of the same shade. The lower part of the bedice was of the dark clo h. while the upper portion was of pale:mauve el() h wit le; n appliqué deign in the darker shade outlined with very five threads of silver. Above this again there was a chernisette of tucked white satin, finished with avery high collar of the same fabric. The inordinately high cellars are very characteristie of the gowns destined for early spring wear. Here is a cement for broken china and glass which is nearly colnurless,thus rendering the crack or join almost invisible :—Dissolve half an ounce of gum acecia, in a wineglassful of boiling water, add plaster of Paris sufficient to form a thick paste; and apply with a brush to the edges of the broken parts. Hold the pieces care- fully toeether until the cement has hardened sufficiently for them to adhere. If the article to be mended is broken in s-veral pieces, do not attempt to cement one fragment before the previous one has thoroughly hardened, eren if a badly fractured object t ikes several days to men d. POTTED SPRATS.—WaSh the fiAli„ t Ike off the heads, and draw the gut. Wash again in salt and water, and dry between two clean cloths. Next, lay the spats in an earthen pan with salt, pepper, and a little pounded mace between es ch layer, and a tow bay leaves between every alternate one. When the pan is nearly full add water and vinegar (half and half) tie a piece of paper over the top, of the pao.and bake re a slow oven. When cold they are fit for use.

"Then it shall be dice tni,tJU kod through another game of caxcli,,," "Very well, dice it shall be. We shan't have to wait so long for the result." By this time so many people stood round the ,contestants that the room seemed literally packed with spectators, who were all doing their best to get a good view of the jewel which was believed to be the only possession that John Mills had left in the world.

There, in a bed of dark crimson velvet, stood a restless stone, of pale blue translucency, clouded with a white fleeciness; and radiating from its apex were six quivering, ever-moving rays of light, that danced upon its surface. It looked not unlike the pole of a blue watery globe, with varying lights of longitude shootini, out in silken flames towards a mythical equator at AS base. It measured nearly five inches round, and was so cut that the hexagonal refraction crossed exactly on the apex of the jewel. When a light was placed on each side of it, three distinct stars appeared, which changed with the movement of the illuminants, and which invested it with a bewildering sulndour.

It does not often' fall to the lot of anyone to see such a rarity as a star-sapphire ‘; but the sight, when once seen, is not easily forgotten, for it leaves an impression of almost supernatural beauty. And it was this treasure which John Mills was willing to sacrifice to his mad passion for gambling! "By Jove!" muttered Mr. Quicke under his breath, "if I can win that for my wife, she will be the•most envied woman in all London," and he bent eagerly down• over the table as John Mills lifted the ivory cubes, and then dropped them tremblingly out of his fingers again. "Two sixes and a five!" exclaimed Lord Alfred Vavasour-Pomeroy, familiarly known as "Ally." "It will take Mr. Rizzen-Quicke all his time to bunt that." _ _

. ..... . "Well, if he does beat it, it will be something phenomenal." agreed the Prince of Mitylene. - And this opinion was shared by the majority of those present. Yet it was destined to be falsified, for Mr. Quiche lifted the dice, and dropped them almost as nervously as his antagonist had done, revealing three sixes as the result of his throw. "Wonderful I"

"Astonishing " "Joseph Rizzen-Quicke may well be called lucky, for no other man living would have been as success- ful as he has been to-night." Such were some of the (minions which were exchanged when it was seen that John Mills's last desperate vent ure had probably left him beggared. There were some who, judging by precedents, fancied that he would break out into loud curses, or that he would utter equally loud lamentations. But he did neither.. He simply rose from the table, pushed his chair back, and stood looking at his host, with his face ghastly pale, and his eyes gleaming with paralysing .despair. "I have been rightly served," he said, his voice so hoarse that he hardly spoke above a whisper. "If I had anything else here to risk, I would still chal- lenge my luck. As it is, all that there is left for me to do is to leave You to the enjoyment of the wealth which was mine when I entered your house to-night." Then he turned his back upon his host, and walked unsteadily towards the door, the other guests silently making room for him to pass. But the winner was not inclined to let matters end that way, and he hastily sprang forward to detain the ruined man. _ _ .

"John Mills," he said heartily, "what do you take me for? Do you think that I would enrich myself by means of the temporary folly of a man who has shared my worries and successes for years ? " "Why shouldn't you, Joe?" was the sullen response. "You won it all fairly, and I have only myself to blame." "Very likely," persisted Joe, "but I don't mean to stick to my winnings. Would you have it said that I invited people here to be fleeced by me? No, no; that's not the sort of man Joe Quicke is; and you shall be as prosperous when you leave this housc., as when you entered it." "Do you mean to say," stammered the incredulous gambler, "that you won't fake your winnings ? " "Certainly I do. If I were not a millionaire already, the income from the Golden Placer would soon make me one; and there is only one thing I will take from you to-night." "And what is that? "

"Your promise never to gamble again." "That is a curious request to come from a man who has provided so liberally for the gambling instincts of his guests," sneered a titled individual whose opinion of human nature had always been pessimistic. Joe heard the remark, but disdained to reply to it, preferring to concentrate his attention upon his partner. "What do you say ? " he urged. 'ditch ? " "You don't ask too much, you give too much," was the wondering reply.- "If it is really true that lam to pay no penalty for my folly, I shall be more than thankful to give you a guarantee. against its repetition, by swearing never to touch cards or dice again." "Then that is all right, old fellow. your hand upon it." "There it is. But you shall not be the only generous man here. I have valued that star- sapphire above anything in the world. But, after all, it will be a small price to pay for the lesson I have had; and if 'you won't take it yourself, I shall give it to your wife." There was a little hesitation on Joseph Quicke's part, which was, however, soon overcome; and henceforth the friendship between him and John Mills was more firmly cemented than it had hitherto been; while a buzz of envy arose among some of the ladies who were present at the ease with which Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke had become possessed of a jewel which was fit to adorn the crown of an empress. If John Mills had learnt a lesson, Joseph Quick° had learnt one too, and while the two friends went in search of Mrs. Quicke, it was decided there and then that the card-room should henceforth become a thing of the past. "We can be grand and fashionable without pandering to vice," remarked the successful gold miner. "And if we cannot find plenty to amuse ourselves with in other ways, we don't deserve any amusement."
"Do I ask too
Give me

CHAPTER IL "DUKE, PRINCE, AND STOCKBROKER." About ten o'clock on the morning following the transference of the star-sapphire to the possession of Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke, two gentlemen were seated in an apartment which was furnished quite as luxuriously as the mansion in Piccadilly, but which differed widely from any room therein, in that it instantly gave the impression of being the abiding- place of someone whose perfect taste was equal to any demands which could be made upon it. Its sumptuousness could hardly be excelled, yet its tones were subdued and restful to the eye, and there was not a corner in it which did not suggest comfort and repose. The carpet was so thick that footfalls fell noiselessly upon it and there were certain signs which indicated that Prince Carlos of Mitylene, the successful gold miner, was occasion- ally fond of quietude. The handsomely-curtained windows were double, and the space between the inner and outer sheets of glass was filled with costly exotics. The doors were also double, and were furnished with rich portieres of bluish-grey velvet. The high mantelpiece, a largos cabinet, and a couple of tables, were good speci- mens of the skill of the Bombay wood-carver. In harmony with these were two or three Rembrandts and a Corregio that hung upon the sunken panels of the wall; and a large, carved ivory dragon occupied the post of honour on the top of the cabinet. Of nick-nacizs, so called, there were practically none; but their presence would only have belittled the regil simplicity of the room': and it would have been difilcult for the most fastidious taste to fine any fault with the tout ensemble. The chairs and , lounges were marvels of upholstering skill, and this was particularly the ease with a delightful-looking t armchair, which stood almost in the centre of the room. It was, however, not occupied at present, for the Prince and his visitor sai, some distance away from it, at a little table upon which stood a silver tray containing an assortment of liqueurs and glasses. they were both smoking expensive Havanas, and they were apparently on very familiar terms with each other. "What do you think of our friend, Joseph Rizzen-Quicke, Esq ? " was the question which the Prince addressed to his visitor, .the Duke Otto von Hapsburg Solltesein. "What do Ithink of him? I hardly think it is necessary for you to ask the question, since my opinion of him is sure to be a corollary of your own. He is quixotic--" "Therefore worthy of our attention." "He is popular just now." "Therefore still more worthy of our attention." "He is exceedingly wealthy." "Greatest recommendation of all I " "Just so. There is no need to enumerate any minor claims which he may have upon our con-

BY MRS. GEORGE CORBETT, Author of "When the Sea Gives up its Dead," "The Prince Physician," "The Vindication of Olive Trevethick, ' "The Star of Yukon," "The Adventures of an Ugly Girl," "Deb o' Mally's," "A Fair Blockade Runner," &c.
CHAPTER I.
" THE RESTLESS STAR. "
"I've had enough of this sort of trifling. Let's play for a stake that is worth playing for."

_ _ "Don't you think it is high time we gave over? Luck is against you to-night, and you have lost your nerve, so to go on playing would only mean making things worse for you." "Luck has been against me so far, but luck .never stays long with one man, and it may leave you for me again. Anyhow, I don't mean to give in, and to shew you whether I have lost my nerve or not, we will change the game to one that requires a little calculating." "Very well • what shall it be ? "

"Bezique." "Bezique! Whoever heard tell of anybody gambling at bezique ? Why, it's only a drawing- room game." "Nevertheless, I choose to play bezique, if you know anything about it; and you are bound to give me a chance of winning back what I have lost to you." "As you please, Mills. be?"
What shall the stake
"We will stake our interest in the 'Golden Placer.' "

"You are mad We each own a quarter interest in that mine, and I don't suppose that interest is worth less than a million of money to us. Think of something else." "No, I will not. Either we play for the 'Golden Placer,' or I proclaim you to be a cad, who invites people to his house, incites them to gamble with him, wins all their accumulated savings, and then denies them their revenge." Mr. Joseph Rizzen-Quicke, the gentleman who was thus contemptuously addressed, felt that his honour demanded an immediate settlement of the matter in dispute, and, without a moment's hesita- tion, he prepared to fight for the tremendous stake at issue. He had really been playing for some time under protest. But outsiders would be hardly likely to believe this, in face of the fact that he prided himself upon the complete equipment of his gorgeous card-room, in which there certainly was every facility for enabling money to change hands, although actual gambling was only resorted to at the special request of players who could see no fun in entering upon games without the stimulus of the chance of winning money. Mr. Mills would doubtless be able to vindicate his assertion that he had not lost his nerve. But the ill-luck which had dogged him all the night had excited him considerably, and he spoke in an antipathetic tone which attracted the attention of all the other people in the room, among these being some of Mr. Quicke's most distinguished guests. The season was mid-summer; the time, two o'clock in the morning; the scene, a magnificent mansion in Piccadilly; and the occasion a brilliant reception, which was the culminating point of Mrs. Joseph Rizzen-Quicke's ambition. A fabulous amount of money had been spent in making the affair gorgeous enough to dazzle the eyes even of people who were used to moving about in scenes of splendour, and although she was almost tired to death with her multifarious duties, the hostess felt proudly elated at the wonderful success which had attended her efforts._ _

Mrs. Quicke was a clever woman, and she shewed herself cleverer than most people by recognising her own limitations. Wherever she had felt her judgment to be at fault she had solved the imme- diate difficulty by givinc, carte blanche to someone who knew exactly the right thing to do, the result being that the sumptuously-furnished mansion had been so beautified by flowers and electric lights that it could very aptly be compared to fairyland. The guests were numerous and distinguished; the caterers had done their work to perfection. The artists who had been engaged to amuse those who had no inclination to patronise the ball-room were the most expensive and popular of their kind, and everything was going as merry as a marriage bell except in the card-room, where the host of the evening was neglecting his general duties for the dangerous pleasure of gambling. This card-room was a luxurious lounge, which was patronised by several people who had not the slightest desire to lose their heads over a game pf cards, but who were, nevertheless, sufficiently amused by watching the various emotions which flitted over the faces of the actual players. Among these were three personages who were subsequently destined to play a highly important part in this drama of real life, and they all gazed with increased excitement while the cards were shuffled and dealt. Just before beginning to play, Mr. Rizzen- Quicke, hitherto always called "Joe Quicke" by his familiars, made a faint attempt at protest. But he proceeded with the game without more ado when his erstwhile friendly partner, John Mills, angrily remarking that it was time to begin, turned up the first card. There was this difference between the two players. John Mills was staking his sole source of income. Joe Quicke had half a dozen other irons in the fire, all equally as good; and comparative coolness was an easier achievement for him than it was for his excited and•reckless antagonist. The first card turned up was the seven of spades, and Mills scored ten to begin with. Quicke held good cards, but he had not a declaration in his hands for some time, while his opponent seemed to have every combination that would count, finishing the hand with a score of four hundred versus one hundred and ninety. In the next hand Quicke declared sequence, and scored six hundred and twenty, Mills being still in advance, wiith a total of eight hundred and thirty. By this time even the spectators were getting excited, for although some of them were quite used to seeing big things in gambling, this was certainly the most formidable game they had ever watched. Quicke was still feeling cool, for it had become an almost accepted belief with him that failure in any important undertaking of his was impossible. But John Mills's face was as white as death, for this game meant all or nothing to him, and his soul was turning sick with the conviction that the ill- luck which had recently dogged him was about to culminate in ghastly ruin, even though the score was, as yet, to his credit. One more hand would see the game finished, and the spectators saw very little chance of its terminating in Mr. Quicke 's favour. Yet excite- meat waxed higher as one declaration after another was made. until, when only a few cards were left, the score stood at nine hundred and ninety to Mr. Mills. and eight hundred and eighty to Mr. Quicke. The latter held four aces, two of them trumps. Could he but declare these at once, it was still possible for him to win, and upon the next card depended all his future. So stupendous was the importance of that card now, that even Mr. Quicke hesitated to lift it from the table, and his opponent glared at it as though it were a phantom which threatened him with immediate destruction.. When at last it was turned up he uttered a groan of despair, for it was the ten of trumps! This meant that the game was saved for the man who could best afford to lose it, and he smiled as he played his ten, which could not be beaten, for he held both the trump aces. Then he declared his aces, raising his score to nine hundred and ninety, following this up by playing an ace of trumps, thus winning the game almost miraculously. The silence with which the spectators had watched the cont?st broke up into a limn of exile- meat at this extraordinary finish, .and John Al ilia brought his fist down heavily upon the oolislied mahogany surface of the card-table. "You have won the game," he said hoarsely, "hut you have not done with me yet! I still have something else to stake. See if your luck can win that from me, too." There was a murmur of rentonstrame from more than one individual, and Joseph Qui, ke protested that, this folly had gone far enough. But his persistent ill-lu,•:: had maddened the losr, and he resolutely declined to allow matters to rest as they

were. Putting his hand into his inner coat pocket he brOught out a small morocco case, and, opening it, disclosed to view a gem whose beauty and rarity were so remarkable that everyone gazed upon it with eager interest. "I have invested .a good many thousands of pounds in the purchase of that jewel," said- John Mills, "and there is hut one in the.whole world that can compare with it.. It is a star-sapphire, and weighs five times as much •as the Queen's wonderful Koh+nbor dAmond. What will you ztake against it ? " "I will stake my nnwly-won interest in the 'Golden Plecer, ' " was the reply. _
sideration, and 1 do not think_ that he should

prove very difficult to deal with." "On the contrary, he is highly amenable tc3 flattery, and, metaphorically speaking, he can easil be twisted round the little finger of anyone who considers it desirable to manipulate him." "That partner of his is an odd fellow, too, ,with a temperament which can be moulded at will-" "By a beautiful woman." "Eractly I I imagine that he would be very susceptible to the fascinations of Princess Delilah. It is doubtful if that wonderful star-sapphire would have been bestowed upon the wealthy but common- place wife of our latest financial success if Mr. John Mills had been previously subjected to the magnetic charms of our supposed Russian friend, your sister." "Yes, it makes one sorry to think so beautiful a jewel should waste its splendour upon a woman who, if report speaks truly, was at one time con- strained to eke out an honest subsistence by letting lodgings." "Hush!- We don't mention those things now that we are millionaires. Let the dead past bury its dead. There can no longer be any recognise' connection between Mrs. Quicke, the lodging-house keeper, and Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke, the wife of the lucky magnate whose financial exploits are the envy and admiration of every poor brainless beggar whf' would fain learn to do likewise. If Joseph Rizzen- Quicke speculates too rashly, and falls headlong from his giddy pinnacle of prosperity, it will no doubt be very wisely asserted that he and his wife have found their true level again; but at present they are so very thickly coated with the glamour of wealth that even the Duke von Hapsburg Solltesein and the Prince Carlos of Mitylene felt quite flattered at being privileged to attend a reception of theirs. And so it will always be. The much- belauded maxim which asserts that' Charity covers a multitude of sins' requires a little revision. Charity only covers some very minor failings; but wealth can gloss over nearly every sin that is men- tioned in the Decalogue." "Discretion is an even better cover than wealth," retorted the Duke; "and the two together are powerful enough to carry the world before them." "Suppose we add the attractions of a noble name and an untarnished reputation, and we may consider ourselves invincible."
"Quite so. There is still one thing -which is impervious to even all these advantages. "Indeed. I should like to hear what that is? "

"A woman's heart. It is the most mystical! thing in creation, and delights in flouting every known tenet of belief. Whoever would have imagined that the dainty Lady Flora Vavasour Pomeroy would have been able to resist the attrac- tions of so highly-favoured a mortal as Prince Carlos of Mitylene ? " "Enough!" was the impatient rejoinder. "The, admiration I feel for Lady Flora is a private affair of my own; and although there is very little else upon which you and I are not in harmony, I prefer• to leave my personal predilections undiscussed." "You are hipped, my friend, or you would not throw my sympathy back into my face. I have never been in love myself, but I have seen its effecta. upon others; and am prepared to make due allow- ance for the variations of temper which it produces. But, to change the subject, doesn't it strike you as. nearly time for Mr. Mosenthal to put in an appear- ance ? "

"He has still two minutes to the good," answered the Prince, "and he has the reputation of being the most punctual man on the London Stock Ex- change; so I daresay we shall see him directly." Even as Prince Carlos was speaking, the faint chiming of a musical gong reverberated through the room, and he turned hastily to look at a small indicator which was fixed in the wall, just below one of the electric light brackets. The dial finger pointed to a sign which was understood to convey the intimation that a gentleman had called to see Prince Carlos of Mitylene. By touching one of the circular ivory buttons which surrounded the dial, the Prince was able to direct his confidential atten- dant to bring the visitor's card in. But even then it would have been impossible for this to have been done if the pressure of another button had not released an electric bolt, which at all times pre- vented the room from being unexpectedly intruded

into. Having satisfied himself that the gentleman who desired an audience of him was none other than the Mr. Mosenthal with whom he had an appoint- ment, the Prince cast away his air of cynical insouciance, and advanced to meet his guest with such a cordial mien that the stockbroker felt highly flattered. "It is very good of you to give a portion of your valuable time to me and my affairs," smiled the Prince, "for I am sure I could not have done such good business as I have lately without your assist- ance." • "Don't mention it, Prince," was the gratified' reply. "I am proud to be of service to a gentleman who is so pleasant to deal with as you are." "My friend, the Duke of Solltesein," the Prince continued, "has always told me what a bad hand I am at business; but he admits that I scored one when I adopted you as my financial guide. Isn't that so, Otto? " Thus directly addressed, the Duke stepped for- ward and extended his hand in greeting to the stockbroker. "How do you do ?" he inquired affably. "I have not had the pleasure of meeting you before; but I have heard so much of you from my friend, that I feel as if I had known you for months." "Oh, lor 1" thought Mr. Mosenthal, treating the Duke's outstretched hand to such a vice-like grip that its owner winced with pain. "Oh, lor ! just to think of a real live dook bein' glad to get to know Sammie Mosenthal! I thought I was gettin' on in the world when I left the old do's shop, off Bishopsgate, and started a pawnshop in Mile End- road; but pawnshops ain't in it with stockbrokin' and 'obriobbin' with lords, and dooks, and eyalty " "Don't mention it," he said aloud. "If it's a pleasure to you, dook, it's more'n a pleasure to me, cos I've heard his 'lghness mention you, friendly- _

many a time." - "Sit down, Mosenthal," invited the host, "and have a cigar while we talk business over. What will you have to drink to it ? " The cigar was an attraction which Mr. Mosenthal felt unable to resist; but he had laid down a rule, years ago, never to muddle his head by imbibing intoxicating drinks during business hours; and he had rigidly adhered to this rule ever since. So, though refreshments were warmly pressed upon him, he politely declined them, and concentrated his attention strictly upon the business which had brought him thither. "I have seen Lord Whitaker and Sir Thomas Bykeman, and for the consideration already men- tioned, plus two-and-a-half per cent of the shares allotted, they are willing to sit on the board of directors." "Then our list is complete now," said the Prince. "We shall be able to issue the prospectus as saw_ as we can-get it printed." "No, sir; there is a little disappointment. Two of the gentlemen that I thought was quite safe have written to say that, after all, they would rather not have anythin' to do with the business, as they can't afford to be mixed up with another failure yet awhile. But I have somebody else in my heye, who, I think, will tackle the job. Their names are just as good as the others; and they are so hard- up just now that they will be glad to snap at a few thousand pounds, which we can offer them as an incloocement." "But are their names as g9od ? " "Well, one of them's he Markis of Spendem, and the other is Lord I:carty." "That will do," assented Prince Carlos. "They are both scamps—but the public doesn't know that —and their names will draw very well." Mr. Mosenthal thought so too, and he stayed half-an-hour to further elaborate the launching of a limited liability company, which was to be entitled "The Electrolytic Goldmakers Company." It was to be capitalised at two million pounds, in shares of one pound each; and it was a foregone conclusion with its promoters that very little of the money would ever return to the possession of its original owners. In other words, the whole project was a colossal fraud, the success of which was none the lees assured because it required skill and daring to carry it out. Mr. Sammie Mosenthal rejoice( . have found such able and willing coadjutors as the Duke Otto von Hapsburg Solltesein and the Prince ot Mitylene. But had he had but the faintest premoni- tion of the ghastly manner in which his association with them was to terminate, he would have fled from their presence with more horror than the vague itself would have inspired. (To lit continued.)

div.head: CRUSADE OF PEACE.
div.p: THE CRUSADE OF PEACE.
A summoNs TO THE TION.
A PERSONAL APPEAL BY MV
W. T. STEAD.

The Crusade of Peace is a movement which needs your help, and which, I hope, if you will read this article through to the close, will receive your help. It is, no doubt, extremely unusual for any representative body of private citizens to take the initiative in addressing such an appeal to their fellow-countrymen, as that which has been signed on behalf of the General Committee of the Crusade by Dr. Creighton, the Bishop of London. But the circumstances are also extremely unusual. Never before, in the history of the world, has there been such an opportunity as that which is now offered to the Nations of striking a heavy blow against one of the greatest curses of the world. Nothing but so grave a danger would have brought into line the representatives of all the Christian Churches, with all the various societies, trades' unions, and other organisations which are repre- sented on the General Committee. The wrangles of party, and the differences of sect are hushed in the presence of a grave peril which confronts us, and of the great hope which has arisen as to the possibility of deliverance. But before proceeding to explain how or why this summons should be issued I had better print here the very words of the appeal which is addressed to every person of influence in the country, over the signature of the Bishop of London.

"We appeal to our fellow-citizens, especially to all those in positions of influence and authority, on a subject of the gravest importance to our national and social life. "The Emperor of Russia, by inviting the Government to a conference to arrest the growth of armaments, gives the peoples an opportunity of which it is ,their manifest duty to take prompt advantage. In the words of John Morley: Never was the moment more opportune.' "By the resolute and zealous co-operation of public opinion, expressed with no uncertain sound through it recognised channels of the Press, the pulpit, and the platforir, and by the votes of representative bodies, the noble initiative of the Emperor will be crowned with success, and the Peace Conference will realise the fruitful results which it is designed to secure. "We would, therefore, earnestly recommend that no time should be lost in making the response of the nations manifest, audible, and universal by every available constitutional means, especially by town and district meetings sum- moned by the mayors or chairmen on requisition of the householders for the purpose of passing resolutions: (1) In support of the objects of the Rescript; (2) To strengthen her Majesty's Minis- ters in their expressed intention of giving ener- getic and hearty support to the proposals of the Emperor; (3) To elect representatives to the national convention charged with the arrangement of the international pilgrimage of peace. "We, therefore, earnestly appeal .to all ow fellow-citizens, acting without party or sectarian bias, to co-operate as speedily as possible in the effort now being made to secure such a vigorous and comprehensive expression of the will of the people as will assure to her Majesty's Government the support of the nation in realising the earnest desire of the Czar that 'something practical shall be done.'" Signed on behalf of the General Committeo the BISHOP OF LONDON. Head Offices: Talbot House, 9, Arundel-street, Strand, London, W.C. • Chairman of Committee: The Bishop of Londork Hon. Treasurer The Marquis of Bristol.

That explains why this Crusade has been pro- claimed, and that describes also the method in which it is hoped that all those who love their fellow-men, and care for the mending of the evil conditions under which they live, should co-operate in producing an expression of national opinion both emphatic and overwhelming. The necessity for such a demonstration at present is because the diplomatists generally are sceptical about anything being done. They say that the Conference will only end in a mere exchange of pious platitudes, because there is no motive force behind it strong enough to insist that something should be done. What we wish to do by this appeal to the country is to create that force, to bring out the latent desire for peace and for the reduction of armaments to the surface, so that all men may see and recognise what is the people's will. Emperors, and kings, and plenipotentiaries are all utterly powerless in this matter, unless behind them stands arrayed the peoples of the world, passionate for peace, and earnest to secure some relief for the increasing burden of their armaments.

Pray, understand, there is no question of dis- banding armies or of dismantling the ships. What is proposed is far more simple than this. The armies and the navies of Europe alone have increased so much in the last thirty years, that the cost has nearly doubled. Before the Franco- German War, the cost of the Armed Peace was about 120 millions sterling; it is now 230 millions, and, what is worse, the increase is ever going on more and more rapidly. If nothing is done to stop it it will double again in thirty years, unless what is still more probable takes place before then, and a great war breaks out, which will involve all the nations in bankruptcy, and ruin, and bloodshed.

The Emperor does not propose to interfere in any way with the full Sovereign liberty of England, or of any of the nations, but only says we are all of us drifting to destruction. The game of beggar-my-neighbour, which is going on at present, is one which must be kept up until there is a general agreement to stop. What the Emperor asks, is that all the Governments should meet together in a friendly Conference to discuss whether the time has not come to stop, and to arrange, if possible, for some way of settling differences that will be better than general slaughter. His proposal is so sensible, so practical, and so simple, that it is difficult to see that any rational man or woman can object to it. And that, strange to say, is just the worst of it, for no one objects, but no one enthusiastically supports. What we want is to take advantage of this golden opportunity and to declare that, in so far as lies within the power of the British people, we shall do our very utmost to he, the Czar and to put the good work through. - If we act, and act with vigour, act altogether, there is no knowing what incalculable good will result among the other nations. Hitherto, no one has ventured to hope that anything could be done. The peoples who were ground down beneath the terrible blood-tax of conscription on the Continent, which takes the young men from their homes and reduces them to what is practically military slavery for two, or three, or four years, have until now not ventured to believe that any relief was possible to them in their lifetime. But now, if the great autocrat of the East of Europe finds his noble proposal cordially supported by the great democracy in the West of Europe, a new hope would dawn like the rising sun upon the nations of the world. Now, it is for you who read these lines, each of you in your own locality, and according to the measure of your own influence, to decide whether or not this great opportunity shall be wasted or whether, in so far as lies in your power, it shall be utilised to the uttermost.

PNEUMONIA AND LUNG TROUBLES.
A Startling Cure at Salford.

MR. THOMAS JUDD (says a "special in the Salford Chronicle) is a single young fellow, residing at 64, Robert Hall-street, Salford. His daily work lies among horses, but he is well-known in the district of Ordsall as an exponent of popular vocal music. By way of introduction, let it be said that the interviewer, contrary to expectation, found in him not the slightest trace of the invalid, but a strong, hearty, .well set-up young fellow. "The beginning of my illness," said Mr. Judd, "was on a Sunday. In the morning I went to look after the horses, and at that time I felt as well as ever. After dinner I lay down on the couch, and on awakening I experienced a sharp pain in the right shoulder. This I attributed to a touch of rheumatism, and thinking it would soon disappear of its own accord, I did not trouble myself about it just then. But in place of getting better it became worse, and I was obliged to go to bed. I was now beginning to realise that the trouble was more serious than I had bargained for. Feverishness set in, and towards midnight my condition had become so bad that it was found necessary to summon the doctor, but it was not until the next morning that he attended, and in the meantime I passed a very bad night." "Did he say what was the matter with you ?" "Yes, he said I was suffering from Pneumonia and Inflammation o'f the Lungs. He said the case was a bad one, and that it would take him all his time, with good nursing into the bargain, to pull me through. After five weeks in bed, I got up in a terribly weak and emaciated condition. I had actually lost 44 lbs. weight in that short period, so you may judge for yourself what a scarecrow I was. What particularly troubled me at the time was the fact that the pain in the shoulder was still there, and that I had a terrible cough, accompanied by difficulty in breathing.

div.head: AGED PEOPLE'S TREAT. OLD MEN' DINNER,
div.p: THE AGED PEOPLE'S TREAT. OLD MEN' DINNER,

On Thursday last week the annual dinner to the old men of Warrington was given ia Parr Hall. It was no doubt owing to the exceptionally mild weather which has prevailed of late that such a comparatively small number sat down. Altogether 312 partook of the good, wholesome dinner pro- vided. The two eldest present were 87 years of age, and the others ranged from 60 to 86 years. The repast consisted of roast beef, mutton, pork, &c., with vegetables followed by plum pudding (of which there was Icwt. cooked), cheese, beer, and tobacco. Afterwards each man was presented with three tickets, each representing a glass of beer or tobacco, and which would be honoured at any public-house in the town for a month. Great credit was due to Mr. and Mrs. Richard Shackleton, of Stockton Heath who had been entrusted with the catering. The platform had been decorated with plants from the Town Hall gardens, kindly lent for the occasion by Councillor Dr. Cannel! (deputy chairman of the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee). Mr. W. S. Woods, (organist at Parish Church), played an excellent selection of music during dinner which was on the tables from 12 to one o'clock The members of the committee, are us follows, all being present with the exception of one or two :—President, Alderman Sutton; vice-presidents, Messrs. D. Jones and Peter Caldwell ;bon. treasurer, Mr. Peter Chrimes ; lion secretary, the Mayor (Alderman J. E. Wright), and assistant hon secretary, Mr. T. A. Sutton; and Messrs. James Smethurst, A. Woods, T. Burton Alfred Jolley, D. Fanshaw, George Pilling, Harry Toft, A. Browne, W. Gill, Charles Bunch, W. J. Forshaw, and Richard Shackleton. In addition to theikives and friends of the members of the committee there were also present :—Aldermen Fairclough and Holmes, and the Revs EC E Carleton, El V Pigot, H'R Wild. Fathers Wilson, Polding and Whittle, and Messrs Richard Shackleon, W J Forshaw, William Dooley, Harry Dooley, G Holford, W J Hooper, W H J Jenkins. H Hoult, Walter Potter,Gearge Watkins Henry Thornton, L Macauley, George Bartley, George Gill, Sutton, jun., John Harrison, Litton, John Sampson Stanley Wright, T B IVlalkin, Joseph H Day, Bush, Strettle, T J Garnett, F 11 Ankland, and Reid. After dinner at which all present had assisted in some way and when the old folks had settled down to enjoy- ing their tobacco and beer, and looked extremely com- fortable, The Rev. B. C. E. CARLET3N said he wished them all a very happy New Year. It was their duty to convey their thanks to the members of the committee, the sub- Fcribers, and the ladies and gentlemen who had given their assistance. It had ben a labour of love with the committee, and they should express their best thanks to them for what they had done. He hoped they would all live to take part in the occasion next year. Father WHITTLE said a man had been refused a ticket at the doors because it WaS only for people who were about 60 years of age. He (Fattier Whittle) remarked that he was 60 and was then asked how he could prove it. (Laughter.) He said he had his certificate. (Laugh- ter.) However they gave the man a ticket. They were very grateful to the committee for giving them such a goad dinner and he hoped to see them all next year. Mr. PETER CHEMISE said he was very glad to see so many old faces. He was the oldest member of the com- mittee and when he came to look round the company lie must say there were more, told men than they had had before—real genuine old men. He wished them all a very happy new year. The MAYOR remarked he did not care if the number did decrease on previous years. They had much to be thankful for and he did not wish to see such signs of distren as an increased number would show, though they were always very welcome. One of the company then proposed a vote of thanks to the committee and all who ha l assisted in any way. The vote was seconded and carried with cheers. _
• A few vocal items were then given before the pro- ceedings were concluded by the singing of the National Anthem.

BANXRUPTCY OF A WARRINGTON BRICIIMAK,R AND BUILDER.—Joseph Welsby, residing at 80, Ellesmere- street, Warrington, and carrying on business as a brick- maker and builder, at Howley Brickfields, Howley, War- rington, appeared for his first public examination in bankrupcy. The gross liabilities amounted to £4,818 19s. 9J., of which sum £4.298 193. 4d. was owing to one creditor. fully secured. The assets are estimated to pro- duce £505 6s. oi,, leaving a surplus of assets over liabilities of £2 15s. 7d. In his observatiens the Official Recriver gave the caus-s of failure, as alleged by bank- rupt :—" My ill.bealth ; an accident to my ribs ; expense of a large family." The bankrupt ststed that he began brickmaking in 1890, with about £lOO capital. Ele commenc d building houses about 1895 ; lost the brickyard last autumn; had kept neither cash book nor ledger, nor, during past three years, made out any balance sheets or statemeats of avets and liabilities. He first knew of his insolvency it April, 1898, and had since contracted debts now owing. His wife was tenant of 80, Ellsmere-street, because furniture therein (worth about £3O) was hers,having been acquired by her before marriage, and because she carried on business as a ven- dor of sweets:rhere. The unsecured liabilities, except £5O, money lent and interest, were almost wnolly trade liabilities for goods, and work done. The creditor fully secured was mortgagee of 7 houses in Parr-street, 12 houses in Fairclough's-avenue, 9 houses in Ellesmere- street,and 14 (uncompleted) houses in Harbourne-street, all in Warrington, and all leasehold. The Assistant Official Receiver (Mr. Potter) stated that in this matter the bankrupt could neither write nor read and had abVutely no knowledge of his affairs. He ( \lr. Potter) had had great difficulty in obtaining infor- mation. It took him a long time and then he would not have got the information but for the help of a rela- tion of the debtor's. It was quite useless puttinm ques- tions to the debtor becaus3 he was obviously incom- petent toanswer them. The examination was not proceeded with,

Re THOMAS CH&RLES RIGBY.—Thii debtor an- peared for re-examination.—The Assistant Offi- cial Receiver stated that the debtor was ordered to file certain accounts wader a peremptory order of that Court. The accounts had not been made out to his satisfaction and be therefore asked the Regis- trar to make a further order upun the debtor to furnish completo accounts.—fhe debt)r said he thought he had furnished ail that was required.—The Registrar said that was tilt so, and he would make an order for the accounts t) be completed within seven days. A RUNCORN CONFECTIONER'S FAILURE —Elizabeth FOR, confectimer, Hill-street, Rune )rn, appeared for her first public examination in bankruotcy.—The Assistant Official Rec.iver said this matter was a trifling aff air,and as the debtor wls a lady he proposed to close the exam- ination; in its present form.— fhe examination was closed.

div.head: P.S.A. MEETING AT BUCKLEY-S MEET.
div.p: P.S.A. MEETING AT BUCKLEY-S MEET.

The monthly open meeting in connection with the Buckley-street Sunday S3hool P.S.A., was held on Sun- day afternoon. The chair was occupied by Mr. Frank Williams. Mr. Cox (of St. Helens) was the speaker for the afternoon, and gave an excellent aldress, which was listened to very attentively by a large number of mem- bers and friends. During the afternoon Mr. VVorsley blind gentleman of St. Helens) gave two solos in a very effective manner, entitled" Nazareth "and "There is a Green Hill." Master A. Johnson sang "The Holy City," in a prai3eworthy manner. Two recitations were given by Miss E. Cox, entitled "Star aa Crown" and "Only Sixteen." She also renderad a solo, entitled "The R-,11 Call." M. A. Trow was the accompanist, THE VVESLEYAN TWEN riE ra CENTURY SCEIENIE.

At Bold-stret t Wesleyan Church on Sunday evening, the Rev. H. G. Rotets, ministerial vcretary of the Twentieth Century Sch-ene Fund of the Warrington dis- trict, preached on the " Omnipotence of faith in rela- tion to the Twentieth Century Scheme." There was a large congregation. The Twentieth Century Fund, Mr. Roberts said, was to be raised by the small contributions of the multitude, and to-day they were asked to persuade one million Methodists each t) give or collect at least one guinea between January let, 1898, and January Ist, 1901, when the century began. Ono shilling per month would provide one guinea, with a margin of 3e. or 211. per week. It was intended that names and addresses of all subscribers mai collectors should be inscribed upon a Methodist historic roll, whice would be preserved upon the historical documents of the Wesleyan Church. The question had been asked to what purpose was that enor- mous amount of money to be deilcatei. Three hundred thousand pounds would be used for building new chapels, mission halls, and Sunday schools, and homes for the Methodist soldiers and sailors. The little village would net be overlooked, and they must make theft position secure in the villages. This was an ago of great cities, but villages had not lest tee-r significance. Two hundred thousand pounds were to be given for educational work. A new training college for Methed'st scholars who in- tended to enter the teaching profession was to be built for Voluntary schools would be established in places where Nonconformists had no school of their own and where there was no School Board. One hundred thous- and pounds were to be given to foreign missions, and ore hundred thousand pounds to home missionary and temperance werk. A quatter of a million would be spent in London on a central Methodist Hall, which would be the head-cporters of all the great movements of Method- ism. Many considered that to be a very large eqiinete, but they needed a monumental institution in the greatest city of the w ,red worthy of the largest Pr ot•-stant church in the world. They must remember that London was nine Lieerpools, four St. Peterburgs, and tw Con- stantinoples, and the throb of the heart of London was felt throughout the Empire. The Cisildreres Home, in which more than twelve hundred poor children were sheltered, was to receive fifty thousand pounds, which was to be applied in saving all the children of Methodist and other Noncenformi:t parentage from Workhouse schools. That movement would commend itself to the young memern of the church. They trusted the coming year would abolish the gutter children. Their pauper children cost the State three millioe pounds per annum. Save the children, save the nation. He felt that they needed in the Warrinetoe circuit at the close of the century, more enterprise, soul, and enthu- siasm. The faith of their people must be increased. They had been reminded by the matter-of-feet people of the world that they were allocating the Twentieth Cen- tury Fund before it was collected, and they laai been exhorted not to indulge in building castles in the air and counting' the chickens before they were hater.d. , The gosnel of commonses-,, as it delighted to call itself, had reminded the Methodet Church of those maxims. It was the pr,rozative of faith to grasp com- ing events as though they were already pre- sent. heir dreams were divine realities. lie had been pleased with the evidences of quiet and un- demonstrative devotion to the cause of Methodism in Warrington. Might such enthusiasm be sustained ! But thrra were were some people very pessimistic who said it could not be done. Christ would have been very popular with that class of people if He never wanted a contrir ution to any fund. Christianity would be then a very ideal of tass. Too many people wanted a religion that cost nothing. On pleasure, personal gratification, they spent willingly and hay, shly. and for religion the smallest coin was doled out; and then they wondered for the best part of the following year that the world was'not converted. They could not measure the results of faith ; they might as well commence to tabulate a martyr's zeel.Mathodism was now the largest Protestant church in the world. Ira 1801 there were eight million Methodists. Now there w re 28 millions. The passage from one century to ano'her was an event of great signi- ficance. Time was speeding on lie asked them to give the scheme the welcome of loyal Methodist hearts. He bssought the Warrington cirsuit to rise in response to that call and give an honest and ringing "Amen" to the appeal made by the Conference. Special music was rendered, the soloist being Mr. Fanshaw, who was in exeseeet voice, and gave an ad- mirable interpretatioe from " Judas Maecabous " of "I feel the Daity within," and " Arm, arm ! ye brave." Mr. Peter Harrison atle aelempaniel on the organ.

div.head: PARR HALL CONCERT.
div.p: THE PARR HALL CONCERT.

Another of the series of popular smoking concerts was given in Parr Hall, Warriugton, on Saturday evening, before a very large audience. The pro- gramme was excellent in every raspect,and the con- cert proved, undoubtedly, to be the most enjoyable of any given previously this ceason. Perhaps the fact that there has been an interval of some weeks since the list concert contribut: d to the interest aroused by the one on Saturday eveuing,but the ex- cellent company of artistes was the principal "draw." The Probyn Ladies Orche-tra once more oppearad on the Parr Ball platform and were warmly welcomed. Tneir selections, as usual, gave ' great satisfaction, and were encored. Miss Mabel Probyn varied the programme with a plecolo solo " The Deep Blue Sea," which was capitally per- formed and heartily appreciated. A cornet solo was, of course, demanded from:Miss Carrie Probyn, who is looked upon as one of the principal attractions in the visits of the Probyn Orchestra. She gave a finished rendering of "The Holy City," but would, we think, have pleased her hearers better with something after the style of" Take a Pair of Spark- lingEyes,"or the"MarseOlaise."The Holy City"is get- ting—if!such a popular song can—a little bit stale. Mr. Nelsoe Jacksen was the humorist,and his efforts to entertain were completely successful. He cams provided with a trio of brand new mirth-pro- voking anecdotes, and fired them off with the best effect pos,ible. Then again with humorous songs, such as" The Music hail,"" Coming Home," and " Drinking Song" he added to the enjoyment of his hearers, but by far his best effort was the ex- pressive recital he gave of Kipling's " On the road to Mandalay," which evoked a storm of applause. Madame Conway was the only vo.eilist, and her pleasing soprano voice was heard t 3 advantage in " When you forget," "Should he upbraid," and "Coming Thro' the Rye." Encores were very fre- quent during the concert, in fact rather too fre- quent, and we would respectfully invite the audi- ence to examine their programmes before they "go in " for wholesale encoring in the first half of the concert. Owing to the frequent recalls. on Saturday evening, several items had to be omitted, including the 'cello solo by Miss Dora Probyn who is a finished executant on this instrument. Many people were di-appointed at her inability to play, and the public would do well to bear in mind the fact that they are not serving their own interests best by getting double the allotted quantity of en- tertainment before the interval.

In the Unitarian Year Book, just issued, there is a record of the deaths during 1898 of 92 eminent members of that denemination. Hivieita the Quakers have had the reputation of being the longest lived of the various sects, but this statement shows that ths Unitarians are likely to go ahead of them in this respect. In the list referred to, 68. or three quarters of the whole number. taking from 69 upward:, average 80 sears, while the ra- maining 24, or a quarter, average 58 years. Taking all round the average for the 92 i 74 years.
