div.head: EXA MIN ER ,
div.p: THE EXA MIN ER ,
JANUARY 13th, 1E99.

WILL there be any Minis- ' Amending the Com-terial attempt to amend —we pensation Act. do not venture to say extend —the Workmen's Compensation Act in the coming session? We think not. Most of the supporters of the Government would regard such a step as premature. The Act will have only been in force about eight months when Parliament meets, and to propose to seriously amend its provisions would be premature. Some of the defects exposed in its working have been very awkward and serious. No one seems to be much enamoured of it. Opposi- tion critics were thought to be extreme when they said it would create a large volume of discontent, and that endless litigation would result from it. They are, however, proving to be very true pro- phets. It may even be said that the most extreme condemnation of it, which said that every clause would have to be tested in several courts of law before it would be settled,is likely to be accurate. In Mr. PICKARD'S address to the Miners' Federa- tion the Act is described as contentious, fruitful in litigation, and "most harmful in creating, bad feeling." He even th )ug:lt it " unworkable.' A collection of the opinions passed upon it by judges would confirm these views. The Act bristles with contentious points. Some good awards have been made under it, however, and they ought to be kept in mind. In the case of deaths, widows have received sums of money under it they could not have obtained before. But the benefits expected in other respects have not accrued. The simple uniformity, the promptness and certainty expected, have been conspicuous by their absence. Many adjudications under it have been wholly unsatisfactory. Certain companies are trying to rope in their employes into other schemes by no means as liberal in general pro- visions. But there will be no time to make amendments next session. The Government is understood to be averse to any efforts in this direction. But it cannot prevent its fol- lowers and other politicians from making the attempt to amend it by private members' bills. Such bills, however, can be blocked and smothered without mercy, under the new system of Parliamentary coercion. That will be their fate, undoubtedly. But the general public must draw, in this instance as in many others that have pre- ceded it, the conclusion that Conservative social and political reforms always limp and prove unsatisfactory. The discontinuances of the ser- vices of men who are getting elderly, or who have any bodily defect, which the Act has brought about, is a very serious one, because it will throw a bigger strain on the Poor Law and strengthen the demand for an efficient system of old-age pensions. The Compensation Act, however, has got to be amended, and it has been of no value as a political-capital creator. Some other moves of the same kind appear likely to produce the same results.
THE idea of a federation of The Federation cf trades is growing apace. We Trades.

see masters entering upon an organisation of this federal kind, and using it to prevent individual bargains between employers and their workpeople. The logical result of any movement of this kind must be the federation of allied trades unions, or otherwise very little can be done when a crisis arrives. In a big trade struggle what usually happens is that firms full of profitable work, who have no special dispute with their men, decline to lock out and to act in unison with other firms. These detachments weaken the resistance; and if they grow in number, the mas- ters have to give way. The same thing must occur where unions, allied in character, decline to stop work and to co-operate in some general movement. The value of federation is very much the same in either case. To move large bodies in any given direction, there must be agreement, after consultation, and a common plan. This agreement involves more exhaustive discus- sion than always precedes individual ac- tic u; and the better the federal basis, the less frequently either masters or men would be found engaged in industrial war upon trifles, accidents, or vagne lines of action. Federation is, therefore, to be commended, even though, on the surface, it seems to increase the potentialities of mischief. But a huge war,paralys- ing some great trade, and lasting for a week or two, is surely better than a long war carried to the point of exhaustion, and affecting allied trades as in the South Wales coal trouble. Federation, moreover, seems to provide two great bodies,strong enough to enter upon negotiations upon equal terms, and therefore more likely to bring about an early settlement. Salf-respect leads to respect for others, and when the men's unions are federated the masters' federations will be less inclined to be arbitrary and coercive. Federation has thus many undoubted advantages, and if there are defects, as pecuniary strain and the possible public disservice, we must take the rough with the smooth, and consider the end to be attained rather than individual incidents. To re- sist federation seems to us, accordingly, a most

unwise policy on the part of working-men, and not until the wholo of the trades unions are federated will that movement have reachel the highest possible development. It is usually too late to bring about ,co-operative action when industrial war has commenced. The true idea is to make this war short and severe, in order that neither side may wantonly bring it about for any but seri- ousmatters. Perhaps the next step after federa- tion will be some change in the relations of these individual and general bodies to the State. The incorporation of trades unions has been found ad. visable in New Zealand, and it is open to serious discussion as to why what has answered elsewhere should not be tried at home. If we had compul- sory arbitration this incorporation would be re- quired. Perhaps federation may be an attempt to avoid incorporation and compulsory arbitration. If this be so, reluctance to favour it by objectors to compulsion seems of rather doubtful expedi- ency.

The far-sighted politicians concerned or the supremacy of Great Britain in the commerce of nations are beginning to see what Mr. Courtney pointed out a year ago in his admirable address to a scientific so ciety. The article which is of most account to a manufacturing population is coal, because the price at which it is ottainable is a prime factor in the cost of production. There have been so many discoveries that have revolutionised branches of trade that we need not trouble our- selves in the interests of a remote posterity about the fact that our coalfields are being used up— that geologists know the supply to be limited, and that when it is done,if the conditions of life remain as at present, the people of Great Britain must sink to be one of the least significant and most help- less nations on earth. The quantity easily work- able will outlast our children's grandchildren, and we may hope that those who come after will find ways of meeting changed circumstances. But the fact that comes home to us here and now is that the average cost of coal at the pit's mouth in Great Britain for the last six years was 6s. 11d. per ton, while in the United States the cost was ss. 2d. In ad. ition to this difference of ninepence per ton America has the immense advantage of natural fuel in immense resources of mineral oil, and her inventors are certainly not behind ours in wit in making machinery and developieg it by labour-saving devices. It will be seen at a glance that our real competitor in merchandise is not Germany but America. The contest will not be less keen because it will be friendly, and it behoves us to quicken our powers of production by education to the utmost of our power.

It is with satisfaction that we note the prose— cution of two 'bus-drivers for racing on the Knutsford-road between Latchford and Warring- ton, and their subsequent punishment. A spirit of emulation or rivalry is all very well in its proper place, but that place is not a narrow and busy thoroughfare if the rivalry exists between the drivers of omnibuses owned by different firms. The racing on the Knutsford-road has been very prevalent for some time, and the keenness of the drivers to obtain the lead have been such as to make them totally regardless of the rules of the road. Consequently there have been several minor collisions and some perilously narrow escapes from serious casualties. If you get a couple of the huge 'buses now plying on the Latchford route racing neck and neck there is an infinitesimal amount of room left for all other and sundry vehicles which may desire to pass. Such a con- dition of things has obtained frequently of late, and we are sure that the Chief Constable has earned the gratitute of dozens .of passengers, not necessarily timid, by his determined action. The fin inflicted ought to make 'bus-drivers see that it is not worth their while to imperil the safety of their passengers in order to reach the starting point before a rival.

The final sentence on Lieutenant Wark is more than a little peculiar, and it appears to us a con- fession of weakness on the part of the Home Secre. tary, who has evidently adopted a half and half policy in the hope of couciliat ng, to some extent, everybody. This is not justice by any means. Lieutenant Wark was charged with the murder of Miss Jane Yates, and he was either guilty of the charge or he was not. If he was guilty, then the respital of the death sentence was a mistake; if he was not guilty then he ought to have been allowed to go free, especially after the severe punishment he has already undergone. That he was guilty of the capital charge eems open to grave doubt, and he is therefore, evdn yet, undergoing punishment for his immorality though to a much less extent than Mr. Justice Phillimore intended that he should. Probably Sir Matthew White Ridley was reluctant to grant a free pardon, and thereby ad- minister an unpleasant snub to Mr. Justice Philli. more. We can, of course, only surmise the Home Secretary's reasons, but the case undsubtedly re- fleets seriously on the justice and fairness of our • criminal administration,and emphasises very much the necessity for a Court of Criminal Appeal.

The Corporation of Warrington are making needful and adequate provision for the future,and last week the Council passed a resolu- tion affirming the promotion of a Bill, in the next session of Parliament, for the construction of ad- ditional waterworks and the general improvement of the Borough. There is no immediate demand for the improvements suggested but the Coun- cillors, like wise men, prefer to have the powers in hand so that when the time comes they can be ready for any emergency. The total sum which the Corporation by its:new bill will be empowered to spend is £418,000—truly an enormous figure—and which will raise the indebtedness of the town to al. most a round million pounds. But nearly two-thirds of the money which it is propoqed to have power to borrow will not affect the. rates. The waten undertaking, estimated to cost £82,000, can be carried out for four years at least, without burden- ing the rates to the extent of a penny, so that really the general scheme of improvement is not at all an extravagant one and will confer immense benefits on the community. A ratepayers' meet- ing has yet to be called, when the people them- selves can have a say in the promotion of the Bill, but this ought to be a purely formal matter and not present any difficulties to the Corporation.

The conscientious objectors to vaccination have been few and far between in Warrington and dis- trict. It is probable that the small-pox epidemic of a few years ago afforded a practical illustration! of the value of vaccination, and one that will not readily be forgotten. The measure recently passed by the Conservative Government seems to have displeased moru Liu it has pleased. We eau almost imagine with what gusto the Conservatives would have denounced such a retrograde measure had it been the progeny of a Liberal Government. But as it is the gift of the present infallible administration we hear only a suppressed murmur. Now and again, however, we do get an expression of opinion, as for instance when Alderman Rani.. son characterised it at the Police Court as a most infamous Act of Parliament. Numerous Boards of Guardians are memorialising the Local Govern.. rnent Board with a view to the Act being amen- ded or rescinded, but, of course, it would never do to allow such staunch Conservative constituences as are included in the Warrington Union to express any adverse criticism, and accordingly it was decided that such memorials should "lie on the table."
A MAD. COACH IN COLLISION NEAR, WARRINGTON.

A serious accident occurred early on Saturday morning to the road parcel mail from Liverpool to Manchester, via Warrington. It was coming in thil direction of Warrington from Liverpool, and when nearing Bold bridge, about five miles from Warring- ton, it collided with a telegraph pole. The fog at that time was exceedingly thick, and the accident is thus accounted for. The vehicle was damaged, and was unable to proceed further. The driver escaped unhurt. Waggonettes were procured and t he parcel baskets were brought to Warrington and sent on to Manchester. ASk or CUNNINGHAM HIGH-CI (SS MINERAL WATEHS.—Advt

div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

SH 3 RTHAND WRITERS ASSOCIATION. The weekly 'meetings of the above association were re- sumed on Monday last, when there was a fair attend- ance of members. The evening was profitably and en- joyably spent by a course of speed practice. It was in- timated that the coming session wilt include several lec- tures by local geatlemen,and also one on the typewriter by Mr. Thomason of Crewe. ST. PAUL'S P.S.E. WIDNES. On Saturday night, a large assembly in the Parochial Itooms, was presided over by Captain Whitehead. Mr. Crawshaw, day school lecturer of the C E,T S, gave an instructive address upon" Our Acions." A capital musical programme was also provided, songs being con- tributed toy Misses Owen, and Clare, Messrs. Thompson Compton, Greenwood, and C Hodgson. Messrs Slaerratt, Heady, and Bennett accompanied. MILTON P.S.A. WIDNES. One of the largest attended meetings in connection with the P.S.A. was held on Sunday afternoon, and the new session promises to be a very successful one. Mr. G. Lacy presided, and spoke upon cleanliness of speech. Mr. Shaw, of Runcorn, was highly appreciated in his vocal efforts, and heartily apPlauded. Mr. Sedden's address upon "A True Friend "was listened to with marked interest, and his remarks were well received. A stirring meeting was terminated with the benediction. FIRE ALARM. About a quarter past twelve on Saturday, the fire alarm was sounded upon the discovery of flames in a loft at the back of Mr. W. Collier's premises in Church. street. But although the brigade assembled their ser- vices were luckily not require i, as the flames were ex- tinguished almost as soon as discovered. The damage tone was extremely slight, which is fortunate, as there was a large quantity of hay and other things of a com- bustible nature in the loft. it RUNCORN WESLEYAN CIRCUIT AND THE 20TH :fa CENTURY FUND. On Monday evening a special meeting of the above circuit was held at Si. Paul's Chapel, when the Rev. C. W, L. Christien presided. There were also present : RevsJ. A. B. Malvern, R. J. Clifton, Messrs. G. Bellamy and A. R. Norman, (circuit stewards), F. J. Norman, F. Possnett, and delegates from the several stations in the circuit. The business for which the meeting was con- verted was to take into consideration the contribution to the Wesleyan 20th Century Fund. Excellent speeches Were delivered dealing with the fund. It was decided to try and raise 1,500 guineas in the Runcorn Circuit, but it was generally expressed that at all events 1,000 guineas would be raised. On Sunday in connectnn with the fund services were held in all Wesleyan Chapels throughout the Kingdom. ALLEGED ARSON AT HALEWOOD. At Widnes, on Mmday, Themes Naylor. of the labour- ing type, known as " Fly " Naylor, was charged on remand with setting fire to two haystacks on Mr. John- son's farm at Halewood, on the night of the 24th ult.— Harriet Mote said she saw the fire from the scullery window of her father's house, and ran to give the alarm. Passing tarough the stackyard she saw the figure of a man, and to the best of her belief it was the prisoner. Several witnesses were called to prove that prisoner was seen in the vicinity of the stackyard both before and after the outbreak. When apprehended Naylor said that when he left the Mersey View Hotel at closing time he walked over Ditton Bridge towards Widnes, whereas two witnesses saw him go in the direc- tion oi Hale. Prisoner, who, in reply to the usual caution, said he was not guilty, was committed for trial to the Liverpool Assizes. COSTUME CONCERT AT BETHESDA . The Bethesda lecture Hall was the scene of a bril- liant novelty, which took the form of a Costume Concert, On Thursday and Friday evenings last weak. The pro- gramme included a musical Tableau "The glad New Year" which was tastefully pi-deuced by the following children :—Old year, Arnold Senior; new year, John J Lunt ; fairies, Lily Lister, Flossie Jones ; seasons, A Chringhall, S Cameron, E Handley, M Handley; months, E Lunt, C Heath, N Ellison, J Gowanlock, A Stanway, J hi Houeh, S Hancock, C Lines, B Clare. E Kenyon, L Deakin, F Lunt; followed by Living Pictures, fairy choruses, character songs, &c., the whole being con- cluded with a National Tableau " Britannia." The costumes and • get-up' were productions of the nimble fingers of the lady teachers arid Mrs. Rhodes, whilst the responsibility for the • effects' lay with Messrs. C. Handley, J Rhodes, F W Hatton, upon the whole of whom the production reflected highly. The accompan- ist was Miss Forrester whose maslcal contributions sus- ained the show throughout. FUNERAL OF ONE OP THE BOY'S BRIGADE. On Sunday an imposing spectacle was witnessed when the members f the No. 1 (Camden) and No. 2 (Bruns- wick) Companies of the Wesleyan Boys Brigade, Bun- co n. escorted the mortal remaies of John William Edge-ock (aged 12 years), one of the members of the Camden Company, to their last raging place in Green- way-road Cemetery. Edeecock was a young but !exemplary member of the Brigade, and after a linger- ing illness passed peacefully away on Wednesday morn- ing. Assembling at the house of the deceased the funeral cortege wended its way through Shaw-street to the Cemetery, hsaled by Dr. F. McDougal, dr. D. Bisbrown, and Mr. F. J. Moulton, (headmaster of the Board Schools) ; then came the ceflu, bearing the remains of the deceased, upon which was a beautiful floral anchor—the emblem of the Brigade—borne on the shoulders of his comrades. The Camden Company fol- lowed with arms reversed, and the rear was brought up by the Brunswick Company. At the graveside the funeral service was read by the Rev J A B Malvern. The officers in command of the companies were: Camden, No. 1. Company, Captain J W Woodland, Lieutenants Gittina, and Littlemore, Brunswick. Captain T Leach, and Sergeant Instructor Rushton. The strength of the companies was 74 : Camden 40, and Brunswick 34, rank and lite. The whole of the arrangements were carried out on military lines, an I spoke volume for the good fellowship ef the members of the Boys Brigade. CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL SCHOLARSHIP SCHEME. The Scheme of Scholarships instituted by the Techni- cal Instruction Committee of the Cheshire County Cowie. oil having now been in operation for a period of six years, it has been considered desirable to report how such scheme is fulfilling the ends which the Committee had in view in its institution; as also to show the class of persons who are availing themselves of the Scholar- ships; and bow far it is acting as an" educational ladder" from the elementary schools to higher seats of learning. The importance of the scheme largely con- sists in providing a way for intelligent pupils to pass from the Public Elementary schools to Secondary Schools. there to extend the instruction commenced in the Elementary School. Hence the Sheme of Scholarships commences with Class 1., to enable pupils of either SPR, who have been taught in Public Elementary, or other similar schools, to proceed to Secondary schools. The ,examination for this class is, of at least equal difficulty, to that required to piss the sixth standard of the ethics- lion code in force, and the age of candidates from nit to 144 years. The maximum age has now, however, been reduced to 14, arid notice given that in 1899 it will be reduced to 134 yeas. Full particulars of the results of examinations, and tee awarding of scholarships in tho various classes, are given in the report just issued by the Cheshire County Council, and which is well wortn the perusal of our readers. INTERESTING PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN. On Monday nieht the workers,Sunday School teachers choir, the members of Mr. Shaw's, Mrs. Mack's,and Mr. H. A. Coke's Sunday School claeses, met for their annual levering in connection with the Mersey Mission, and to toe number of about 80 sat down to a well. served tea, which was laid out in the schoolroom. After the tables were cleared the chair was taken by Mr. W. Shaw lc ho thanked all for the assistance and work they bad done during the past year. Having given a resume of the year's work, he said upon occasions of that kind they usually made a presentation to some of thiir friends who bad become wedded, •or who were about to leave them for other work. That night they were going to make a presentation hut he would not say to whom. He would leave that to Mr. Shaw (the superintendent of the Sunday Schoo.), who would also make the presentation. Mr. Snaw (superintendent) in a neat speech referred to the nature of the work they were employed in. It was a voluntary undertaking and he was glad that it was so. There were only two paid persons connected with the Mi:san all the rest was free labour and he thought there was nothing to equal it. Having dealt with the importance of the work of the Sunday School, Mr Shaw said they were about to make some smail recognition of the long and faithful work of one of their co-'corker—Miss Bowyer. (Applause). Miss Bowyer had been connected with the Mission for 15 16 years,and during that time bad labnined assiduously and willingly; and whether employed as mistress or servant she always came up trailing. (Applause) He was pleased to make the pre- sent to Bliss Bowyer as a smal token of the appreciation of her co-workers. (Applaese.)—Miss M. Bowyer, in accepting the beautiful writing desk presented, said she could not find words sufficent to express herself : but thanked them all very much for her pleasant surprise. (Applause). —Mr .J. Stokes then delivered an eloquent address upon the work of the mission, which was toll of advice and encouragement, The meeting was also addressee by Mr. H. A. Cooks, Mr. J. Shaw (organist), send Mrs. Mae,k.—The remaieder of the evening was Apeht in games and other amusements.

div.head: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

The Clerk tooli-ioe chair and havine read the return- ing officer's declaration of the p Al, said the first business of the Board was to appoint its chairman. Mr. E. unison said he hai the name of a gentleman . to submit for the post of Chairman who had taken con- siderable interest in the work of the Board for the last nine years, and who by his counsel hid contri °laced in no small degree to the efficiency of the Board Schods of wlich they were so proud. As chairman of the Educational Committee of the Northern Province, and secretary of the Associa- tion of Church Schools for the Diocese of Chester ; as a school manager, and in fact. Chairman of two or three Boards of Management of Voluntary Schools as well as a member of that Board he had accumulated experience that would fit him for the position, which it was his (the speaker's) pleasure to nominate him to fill. In addi- tion to that—and perhaps it was the most important reason which could 14e given—the ratepayers had re- cently shown their confidence in him in an unmistakable manner. For these reasons he moved Canon Wood's elec- tion as Chairman of the Board for the next twee years. Rev. H. B. Gore seconded. Ha endorsed what Mr. Isnisen had said about Canon Wood. In matters educa- tional he thought they had in the Vicar one who was thoroughly acuainted with every point. Mr. F. J. Norman said thou;h not inclined to question the justice of the appointment the Beard might be des r- ous of making, he :c Arid not refrain from referring to the unhappy circumstances which removed Mr. James Pritchard from the chair. He had sat upon the Board since its formation about a quarter of a century ago,and during half that period he had occupied the chair. The fact that he had not been directly or indirectly connec- ted with any other educatiooal agency had inspired a confidence in his impartiality that he (Mr. Norman) submitted could never be given to any sectarian school manager. His intimate knowledge of their complex dual system had enabled him to hold the balance with perfect adjustment, and as the constitution of the Board had changed from time to time he had kept before it a very high educational standard. He knew that Mr. Pritchard had recently been charged before the public with " wanting ta injure Sectarian schools" and with" not wanting to save the rates." (Mr. Norman here produced one of the election hand- bills issusd by the Church candidate;.) Pioceeding he said slice a charge from those who did net know Mr. Pritchard might be dismissed as ignorance. Such a charge when made by men who did knew him amounted to un`ruth. There were two important fac- tors in Educational matters that public men had now to reckon with. (let) The sordid element in the elector- ate which wou!d sacrifice all the Educational machinery in the country to-morrow if by SI doing testy could " down with the rates." (23d) The sectarian element which was always striving to dam back the educational tide, except such portion of it that they could divert into their own narrow channels. Mr. Pritchard had neither pandered to the one nor fawned to the other and it was thiS precious contamination that overthrew him. Mr. E. Imison thought it was unreasonable to discuss the appointment of chairman from the standpoint thrust on the Board at the pre3ent time. Mr. Norman said his object was to show that Mr. Pritchard had done his duty in that position, it was a rather serious position for-- Mr. E. lerson : It covers a very wide field indeed, and is not relevent to the appointment of chairman or to the submission of an amendment. Mr. Neraran said he would not subnft any amend- ment, and would at once support the resolution ; bet he took that opportunity of saying they had had a clerical election with all its miserahle sophistries,its gross misre- presentation, and its pitiable pandering to that sordid element whica he had already described. He was sorry for this--

Mr. Imison thought that Mr. Norman wAsøill cui- tinning a line of procedure to which he objected. img pause ensued. Mr. Norman said that it was rather surprising to him that Mr. Imison in proposing t )e Rev. Canon Wood dwelt upon the virtues and quali- fications of that gentleman, yet the moment he had any- thin," to say about Mr. Pritchard he was ruled ou'; of order.

_ Mr. unison submitted thst he had not attempted to define the argumints that had been placel before the electors, or the reasons that contributed to bring them there. He simply submitted what he considered to be a legitimate description of till geßtleman he nominated as chairmn, beyond that he did not go. Mr. Norman was practically discussing all that had been b ,fora the e'ec- tors for the last two Months. If he were to answer it he would say that it hal alrealy been answered by the ratspayers, and as a consequence those gentlemen who held those views were present by a majority.

Mr. Ligatburn suggested teat -Mr. Nrminin could say what he bad a parfact right to say about Mr. Pritchard, if he intended proposing an amendment. Mr. Norman said ho would supeort the nomination of Canon Wood. The election was a clerical election; that was the ticket upon which it was won, and in his opinion Canon Wood ought to have the chairmanship of the Board. The reso'ution was put an I unanimously carried (all voting). Canon Wood in taking the chair, said he. could not help saying that he fe't he bad been elected to a highly honourable pest. Add,berides that,it was not easy for one who felt that the welfare of the child was the hope of the c -untry, to occupy such a position, as he did that night, without recognising it as a highly favourable one because to a very great extent, to that Board was com- mitted the welfare of the children of the town for the future. He not only thanked those gentlemen who had kindly proposed,seconded and supported the proposition but he felt that he ought also to offer his thanks to th 3 great majority of the ratepayers of the town whose wish he knew it was that flair should have placed him there. It was his duty to say that he felt he was placed in that position net because of any personal abilities, and Mr. Liaison had spoken of himself more kindly than he aught to have. He represented a very clearly defined policy—a policy that could be defined in two words—efficiency and co-operation.— the efficiency of the schools and of the work generally at that Board was, he was quite sure, the hearty desire of every ratepayer in Runcorn. The ratepayers he be- lieved, approved of the dual system of education; and which was r.presented by the existence of Board and Voluntary Schools side-by-side. He believed it to be a right and peeper positio% and one that commended it- self not only to the ratepayers of Runcorn but to the people of this country. It was not the pelicy of the country to overthrow the old work, but to let the now grow side by side with it. He understood that he took the chair as a representation of that policy. And ho would like to say that it WAS not a new policy of that Bran i but it was, practically the policy that had been followed by the Board ever since he had known it. That policy had been an exceedingly successful one. It was the policy of the Board in Mai past. and Was the policy they were going to co ,tinue with. The friends of the voluntary system of education had, always, in his recollection possessed a majority on the Beard. Then - fore it was right to say there was going to be no change of policy. His being in the chair however, showed thae the friends of the dual system had more cohesion, an i the ratepayers of the town h d a keener appreeiation of the value of thevoluetary schools than ever thee had hef ,re. It was always the characteristic of loyal kindly Enelishmen. whatever m'ght b a their differoncei.to give their support to the chair, and while it was quite true they differed in many matters. yet he hoped in the fu- ture the old happy tradition of the Board might be con- tinued, and that whilst thy met there they would do so in a kindly spirit, without personal hostility,with a good kindly feeling and courtesy one tow 3r35 another, as he believed in that way the work of the Board awl the welfare of the town would be satisfactorily achieved.

MR. HANDLEY REJECTS THE POLICY OF "DOWN WITH TRE RATES "

Mr. im—i-so-n—icr4-3-sed that a Finance Co.r.n.i.-.tee he appointed, that it consist oe the Chairman, Me Hand- ley and himself, and that it meet once every half year, or oftener if r,:wrired. Mr. W Handley said the recent election mainly turned upon the question of expenditure as he understood it. The election was won on that questioa and there was a distinct belief in the town—he spoke with full know- ledge—that the rates were going to he reduced. He could net see his war to be a party :o it. Under other circumstances he should have been glad tl have worked on that Committee. He knew that a canvasser who went round distinctly promised that the rates were to be lowered if cntain gentlemen were returned. (Hear, hear.) Those gentlemen were elected, end he thought they ouc..ht to have the opportunity of lowering the rates. In his opinion it was; IMPOS•ible to keep up the efficiency of the Baari on the least exrenditure. He always looked upon their expenditure as the lowest ex- penditure on thereto; from the fact that education

would lower other expenses. He was willing to spend more on education and far lees on pauperism and prisqps. He knew what hal been the tendency of the E lucatiera Actr, of the past 25 years. They had only something like half the prisons that existed prior to the passing of the Eluca tion Acts. He would very gladly help to do everything he could, but could be no party t "keeping down the rates," if he did he would be casting a very serious reflection on the Beard of the past, and suegesting that they had wasted the money. He believed that the money had been wis3ly spent and perhaps better spent than in mest Owns in the country. Tney had very efficient schools and taking place by place he believed they had been worked at a comparatively less cost than other places. The Chairmaa said he did not like to interrupt, but he thought there was nothing before the meeting. Mr. Handley said his name was before the meeting, and he was giving an explanation. He should b 3 very glad to take part in any work of the Board, but felt he could not acclot responsiUility if what he had stated was to be the policy of the Beard, and it was distinctly understood that the rates were to be reduced. Mr. linison said as it was clear Mr. Handley would not join the Committee, he proposed Mr. Cunningham, the Chairman an I himself constitute the Finance Com- mittee. Mr. Cunningham in seconding, said he would accept the responsibility. Mr. Norman ,aid he would be very glad to support the proposition. Probably at the end of the next three years they would hear what the sophistry meant with regard to "down with the rates." The motion was carried. CORELESP3NDENT The first meeting of the Runcorn school Board affords EOM° interesting reading, and shows that the progressives are quite determined to let the Church party steer their own course. It was rather a pity that Mr F. J. Norman was interrupted, for we might have had much more interesting reading. There was no interruption whatever whilst the merits of the Chairman were being extolled by Mr. lmison, and even if that gentleman dui not quite like listening to Mr. Norman, edit it might have been iuch better for all,and especially the "Clerical party," if they had heard all that was in store for them. As it was Mr. Norman had to stop and for a time the fun lagged.

lir. W. Handley was the one to revive it, but he too, when getting fairly warm, was brought up. Still he hit pretty hard and atraight,and there ought to be no doubt left in the minds of the Board 111901- bets as to what he thinks. It was perhaps a goof stroke on the nart of Mr. Imison to secure him for office on the Finance Committee, bat the way in which he parried the thrust with "I decline the honour" was masterly.

The days of the Voluntary System are un- doubtedly numbered,and there caul:be no mistaking the fact that the whole must give way to an im- perial system of education. Church people them- setves will tire of its antiquity, .its rottenness; and of the fallacy of fighting for a piece of conservatism that is retarding in its effect upon National educa- tion—a fight they are at present engaged in simply under the lead of clergymen whose aim is to retain a means of fostering to their owa beliefs.

(BY ANOTHER CORRESPONDENT.) Anyone reading Canon Wood's speech, made at the School Board meeting on Tuesday night, might be inclined to believe it. He talks of the constitu- tion of the Board being the same .as it was ever since he could remember. On reference to some back numbers of. the "Examiner," however, I fiad that such is not the case, and for the benefit of my readers I will record a little interesting history: —Six years ago the Board was composed of the following gentlemen : Messr3 J Pritchard, Handley, S. Taylor, Imison, Dr. McDougall, Rev. Canon Wood and the Rev. Dr. Gas- taldi. Those were the members; and the analysis works out thus: Messrs. Pritchard, Handley, and Taylor were Nonconformists, Dr. Galtaldi was an Italian with an Italian's love for education. Dr. McDougall stated to canon Wood himself that" he reserved to himself the right of actinz as he thought fit" and styled himself an independent and not a church candidate; the other two Rev. Canon Wood and Mr. Imison were "church" candidates.

It is therefore apparent that the worthy Canon does not give himself credit for what he deserves. lie has won a" clerical election" to use the phrase of Mr. No.man, and now has a following that he never had before; but t 3 say that no change has come over the state of affairs is not quite correct. For a great and terrible change has taken place. On the Board which the Canon first met in" corn- promise" there were four gentlemen who were educationalists fist and religionists afterwards, bat now there are four gentlemen who are religionists (Churchmen) first and educationists afterwards. There can be no doubt that the Vicar knows, as I know,t his was one impartant reason why he did not before fill the coveted chair. He is to be congratu- lated on an ingenious, well-thought out victory, and in securing the Rev. B. B. Gore to assist, has brought shout its coniumruation.

The recalling of the little episode of the" upper room" six years ago which ended in Canon Wood withdrawing the candidature of Mr. Timmins, through the strong position taken up by Dr. McDougall who would have nothing to do with " apostatising " will I think be sufficient to show that all is not forgotten—and some of us are quite aware that a great ct, auge both in constitution as well as policy has occurred.

Farther, Canon Wood goes on to say that the re- moval of Mr. Pritchard is the "fate of war" and not a "personal "affair. Now if the representation is the same, and the policy of the Board the same as of old, and if it ie to continue so, where is the necessity for deposing llr. Pritchaid at all? if it is not a personal ens. The " fate of war," indeed I It resembles more the" bayoneting of a wounded warrior "than anything else,aad not the generosity of a noble foe.
BETHESD.A. P.S.A. 'RUNCORN.

OPEN MEETING On Sunday afternoon an open meeting was he'd in the Bethesda Congregational Chu.ch, under the auspices of the P.S.A. Society. Miss Stella Clegg, of the L melon, Liverpool, and Provincial Concerts, had kindly con- sented to sing, and there was a large attendance. The Rev. J. Osborne presided, and he was eunperted by Mr. eV. H ckman, of VVarringtou, Mr. W. Handley, Mr. F. Beck, and others. Alter devotional exorcises The Chairman said the society was already in its second year, and he could assure them it was in a very flourishing condition. When they thought of the number of addresses that had been given to the men of the soce sty, and of the ye tiety of the solos that had been sung, they could not but come to the conclusion that a very solid influence had been brought to bear upon the lives of those who had been present. Their P.S.A. meetings provided a solid religious service for those men who found it difficult to turn up at the Sunday morning ser- vice. But ,hey did not want them to have the impres- sion that these meetings were to take the place of the morning or evening services. In his ju 'gment, they never could do so. There was about the morning and evening Services a grandeur above that of the Sunday afternoon meetings. They, wanted that society to be a stepping stone to something better. It wets simply to be an institution to lead the members to join themselvea to some church in the town. He trusted teat all he churches in the town—and if he might say so, the Es- tablished Church also—were profiting by the society. They had two or three adaitionel attractions that after- noon, and he was pleased to see so many present t o en- joy tee good things provided. (Applause.) Mr. Hickman, who was cordially received said he had a fatherly interest in their P.S.A. at Runcorn. He was present at its birth, twelve =laths ago. He was there on the last Sunday in January, at its first open meeting, when it was bapt zed—(laughter) —and he was present on that occasion, when it was twelve months old, when it had cut some of its wisdom teeth and c ould begin to walk without his assistanee. (Laughter.) That afternoon he wanted to speak to parents and to children, to those who were baring the burden and heat of the day, and who bad family responsioility, and to his dear young friends. His eueject was" Happy homes, and how to make them." Fist of all, if a looms was to be happy it must have a head in it. That head must be a wise head, one whom the members of the family could trust and feel safe under. The head of the house must be obeyed if the home was te be happy. Next there must be a firm hand in the home. If it was an iron hand it most have on it a velvet glove. There must be discipline in toe home. The hand must be firm enough to rule, and the head must be wise enough to direct. He believed there were more yceing poople spoiled through lack of discipline and softness than anything else. If they allowel their children to become tm years of age before the will was trained they had sown a heritage of sorrow for the rest of their days. There must be in the home a wise head, a firm hand and a warm heart. There must be no tryanny. Wisdom, firmness, and leve,were the three great principles which would help to make a happy home. There must be obedience on the part of the children to the head of the house, and there must also be denial and eelf-sacrifice on the part of the parents. If a home was ta be happy there must be no black sheep, no prodigals in it, no bad boys and no naughty girls. In conclusion, the speaker wished the movement every success, and intimated that he would be glad to visit them again in the courts of a few months. (Applause.) The soloist for the day was Miss Stella Clegg.of Liver- pool, a lady ss he is a welcome figure at P.S.A. gather- ings throughout the country. Her visit to Runcorn was entirely voluntarily, and perhaps ho one felt greater pleasure in the successful proceedings uf the day than Miss Clegg. Toe large audience were evidently antici- pative of a rare musical treat, and in this expectation they were certainly not disappoin-ed. Miss Clegg possesses a rich soprano voice, perfect in its range and compass, and never taxed beyond its legitimate limits. She has also a pleasing presence, which adds mat rially to hay vocal powers. Her first item at the afternoon service was the "Star of Bethlehem." This she rendered with exquisite power,and with a vocal pathos that made itself felt throughout the crowded chapel. Her neat etontribution was that superbly fins specimen øf Handel's genius "Oh, Divine Redeemer." Miss Clegg's treatment of this masterpiece was all that the most eesthetic eritio cou!el desire, and was loudly applauded by the audience. Mr. W. Cooks, A.R.C.-0., was the accompanist, and in his capable and efficient hands the instrumental part of the proceedings was perft ct. It is perhaps only fair to Mr. Cooke to state that his services en the occasion were gratuitous, a fact which the public are not slow to appreciate. At the evening service in Bethesda Chapel Miss Clegg sang by special request. The Rev. J. Osborne occupied the pulpit, and preached an eloquent discoi.rse on " Christ and the sinners." In alluding to Miss Clegg's visit to Runcorn he voiced toe feelings of the congregation generally in saying that much might be gained, spiritually as well as morally, by the lessons often conveyed through the gracious channel of song. Miss Clegg sang twice at night. Her first item was " Angels ever bright and fair," which she rendered in magnific me style, her splendid voice resounding through the chapel, and creating quite a suppressed furore. At the conclusion of the sermon she sang" The Holy City," the tender pathos of which appealed to all present. Mr. Arthur Savage— a local gentleman who is highly respected—was the accompanist at the evening service, and nothing but the highest praise cm be ten lotted to him for his services, which were also free. During her visit to Runcorn Miss Clegg bee been the guest of Mr, and Mrs. Horace Handley.

The accommodation provided in this building for Police Court and other purposes having been found deficient and quite uasuitable for the proper des- patch of business the County Council determined to enlarge the buildings iannindg fporremthisaets pfruormpo;feepssurrs-. Co. upon which the new ex- cehrae ?Lida ‘lvBh9i6t tehyea anddj tension has been erected. The Police Court and inspector's house adjoining which funned the principal portion of the old build- ings have been left intact with the exception of certain interior alterations, but for the convenience of the magistrates, witnesses and others attending the court, a new suite 01 rooms comprising magistrates' retiring room and lavatory, wit- nesses' room and jury rooms have been pro- vided. The Police Court has been entirely rearranged on the most approved plan, and now . contains all necessary in rangements for the comfort and con- venience ot pers-ms attending the courts, in fact this court is one w th 4 best arranged and fitted up Police Courts in the County of Chester. The superintendent in care of this district has been accommodated with a new re iidence looking on to the side street, so arranged as to have proper control over the whole of the Police Department. The building has been designed by Mr. H. Bee- wick of Ceester the architect to the Cheshire County Council,and the contract was originally undertaken by Messrs. A. and H. Ta begin the new year by breaking a record is a novel experience for Warrington, and one they ought to andcavour to repeat. On Saturday. at Wigan, they secured a victory of 8 points to nil, which is a remark- able performance inasmuch as they have never pre- viously, I believe, defeated the Wiganers on their own ground. , Why! there is good hepe for suceess at Run- corn now. If Warrington can thrash a stiff team like Wigan away from home there is no reason whatever why, they should not thrash Runcorn, unless it be that Runcorn are the better lot. That, of course, is rather an important detail. But having broken one recorel,it is to be hoped that they will go on and break others. There is plenty of opportunity. Warrington have yet to win at Oldham, and there will be a chance in the cup-ties. Judging by the form of ViTarrington shown in the League m itch at Oldham on November 19th, there is small hope-for Oldham. Really I feel quite proud of the " wire- pullers " this week, and I wt I now proceed to relate bow they went, saw, and conquered.

Some of thA players went by one train, some by an- other, and some by still another. In fact one haltback travelled round by Mariche,ter and got to Wigan before some of the others. That shows the versality of our railway system. Oace arrived at Wigan. and the travel- ler fees glad,—glad the journey is over—but his joy is as nothing compared to that which he feels on leaving the HAW place. I know of no t3wa which I would sooner leave behind than Wigan. People allude to the griminess and dirtiness of Warrington, but "the good old town " is a veritable Paralise ia comparison with ' Wigan. Talk about mud, and filth, Ugh! you can wallow in it there, and cn a fine day too.

Th 3 ground of the Wigan F.C. is about on a par with the r.st of the town. It is the most dismal place imagin- able in which to play football. What turf there is, is the colour of c3al-lust,and the .tat.ids have a pre-A.dam- it3 appearance which is not very cheering to the visitor. lam afraid the decadenc ot the Wigan club is proceed- in t; apace, to judge from the look of things. Spe3tators are few, probably there were a thousand round the en- closure on Saturday, and the Warrington match is an old favourite with the Wigan folk. Altogsther,ths visit to Wigan was rather depressing and it is a wonder in- deed that Warrington managed to do so well under the circuolscances.

On leaving Warrington I was more than a little dis- mayed to find that" Smack " Bite was unable to play from illness, and my hopes went chwn almost tN zero. The Warrington team h usually very small beer indeed without its captain at the head of affairs, and the result of matches played in his absence is usually dreadful to cont3mplate. Instance—Oldham. But for once the team rose to the occasion, and no doubt inspired by my encouraging remarks last week they slew the Wigasers. I eic,aect it is the" stewing" part of the busin2ss you want to hear about so, here goes

Warrington went off frointhe start with a dash which meant business. Harris and Fish, by the narrowest squeak only, failed to register tries in the first minute. Playing in excellent style the visitors kept the homest.frs on the defensive. Both fore and aft their combina- tion was good and contrasted with the raggedness of Wigan's play. The first score was somewhst delayed, but I felt sure it was coming. Cross ha l the hardest of luck with a clever drop-kick, and then the players were rewarded for their exertions by seeing Dan Isher wood dash Over from a pass by Ashurst. The god-kick went the way of most goal-kicks Warrington have anything to do witn, and at half time the score was one try to nil in favour of Warrington. Play was pretty mach the same in the second half, Warrington's superiority being very manlest. The home defence was good, however, and it was an eye opener when Fish smartly profited by a mull on the part of Winstanley at centre, and ambled easily betweenthe stumps. The try was a " soft" one cer- tainly, but it was well got and does the scorer credit. The Wiganers gasped ; they were content to do that and made no attempt to hook Fish. Isherwood took the goal-kiA himself, and managed to add a goal. Not long after, the home lot were penalised and Hallam tried at goal from a position near the touch line, the ball travel- ling syrsight and true, and hitting the cross-b tr. More hard luck for Warrington ! The score remained natl. tared, though before the close Wigan made a desperate effort to obtain a tangible point. Their combination was so shockingly bad, however, that they were easily repulsed.

On Saturday's form Wigan is the poorest League team which has yet opposed Warciagton. The bseTs were simply at sea and made a tar worse show than did Morecambe when Warrington visited the vaside club. Forward the teams were evenly matchad,wnich is som,- thing to the credit of Warrington, as the Wigan eight were the sup?rior at Wilcierspoal. Warrington played as they did at Swinton, and the dash 6hown more than made up for any lack of weight. Naylor,Boardma.n,Sucl- low, and Tom:tend were the pick of the pack. At half, Ashurst and Duckworth combined excellently, aad both men did a lot towards beating Wigan. Llairwool paved bAter than I have seen him do for a long time. His fielding 3t the ball, running and passing earned tne ' praise 03,703 ot the Wigan spe3taters. Harris and Fish both p'ayed a sound, dashing game and c mtinually troubled the Wigan defence. Cross had little to do, but was safe in emergency Hallam was in fine form, land shone above Winstanlev, the ex-county man, in the way he canght and nturned the ball. He appears to ba im- proving every match,and does less following up on occa- sions when it is needless. Taken all rolled the Warring- ton men played a vastly improved game, but this was due, isa larg 3 measure, t the weakness of the team oppostkto them.

L?igh will he the visitors at Wilderspo9l this Satur- day, and my be relied upon to give Warrington a had d game. Some o the performances of the Leigh club this season have, been truly remarkable, and no h-er than Saturday last they tnok Broughton Rangers down vary decisively. In all departments the L.ighites are strongly reprezeited, and p:esent a good example of what judicious importation can do for a club which is far from being one of the wealthiest. The Warrington team is composed as it was last Saturday, and I cannot see in what reswct it could be improved upon with Vie material at command. The principal weaknesa is still at centre-ttireequarter, and the c -immittee really ought to mak- a strong effort to remedy it. One first class man would make a world of difference in this position. But tak riF,, the teams as thAy are I think Warrin2ton ought to win,always providinz that they play with determina- tion. Last year they nearly lost, Barber saving the game with a magnificent try in the last five minutes. The year before, Leigh defeated Wa7rington, so that the latter yet owe their visitors a grudge.

CRUEL TREATMENT OF A WARRINGTON WOMAN. At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, James Evans, of the Snip Canal barge " Polly," was summone I by his wife Elizebeth Evans, of 2, 0 wen-straet, Dallarn- lane, Warrington, on a charge of persistent cruelty towards hr.—Mr. C. E. Preston, Runcorn, appeared for complainant, whilst the defendant coniucted his own defence.—Mr. Preston, in opening the ease, et stel the parties were married on the 5% July, 1895. Mr. Evans was a waterman. being captain of tee flat" Polly." His wages stood at £1 is a week, but by means of overtime, etc., he was able to increase it to about £1 12s. a week. About nine months after the marriage, the defendant struck her and used obscene laeguage to her, and up other °cessions threw thinesa t her, tore the clothes off her back, and threatsned her; so that she was afraid ef living with him. She tiler:fore asked for a separation and m tintenafce order.—Eliza- beth Evans, the complainant, corroborated the solicitor's opening statement adding that on the sth of December her husband turned her out of the house, and but for some of her friends taking her in the would have been out all night. He had threatened to 'lea her and also t, set the bed on fire. He hal assaulted her several times hitting her en the sides of the head, and had torn the clothes off her back.—Defen- dant: I love my wife. air, and never struck her at ail. Tore her dress ? o! I was too fond of her, sir.—P.C. Gregory stated he knew the deten,lant. On the 29th of April 1898, be was called to his house in Wellington- street. He found Mrs. Evans crying, and the defenden: was creating a big disturbance, in cense q lenC3 of which defendant was locked up and fined 51. and costs. On that occasiea Mrs. Evans had two black eyes caused by her hushand.—Defendant at this juncture alleked that his wife who went by the name of Mrs. Walker was behaving disgracefully, and he kicked a man out of the house that day. He knockad him clean through the entry. (Laughter.)—Witness (to the bench) : I saw him strike his wife.—Defendant pretested saying he came from the most respectable family in Runcorn, and proceethd to give detai.s of the way in which his family ha I been brought up.—P.C. Gregory centinuiag, said on the 26th October. 1895, de- fendant was ain convicted, and again in Octooer for using obscene language.—By the Bench : Mrs. Evans was perfectly sober.—For the defence defendant stated that he had a comfortable home and had always been gaol to his wife, who was the best of women until she got entangl; d wili a lot in Brook-etreet,after which ho could no nothing with her. She left him on the 18te of October in a tipsy cosidi:ion, running away and would not hear him at all. Ho walked te Warrington a et went to the liousl she was at and wanted to se ; her ; but that lide (plating to someone in the Court) met him with a fire poker.—A Voice: "Teat was on Monday.—lle had been rested the world three timee ; toe Hessian War, and the Egyptian War, and gained the medal. He earned a guinea a week, but perhaps hic earaings all round w )uld average a 225, all of which he gave to his wife.--Complainant admitt, d elm got Li 14. —lt was too much money he gave her. He loved his wife and thought a great deal of her and upon marrying her had paid all her deets.—Ele denied the efface( s in tJto.—lo answer to the Bench, Superintendent O'Kell said the woman had not been in any trouble and bore a good characeir as far as they knew.—Mrs. Evans re- c shed said she was quite determined not to live with the man. Sh ; dared net.—An order was made for judicial separation and a msintennce order for 5; a week. Thl 'defendant to pay c )ets.—Defendant said he woull not I pays

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

THEFT BY A DOMESTIC SERVANT.—At the Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday morning, before Messrs. John Ockleston (chairman) and Samuel Taylor. Mary Joynson, a domestic servant was charged in custody with the larceny of a gold finger ring valued £4 103 and a pair of corsets, 93 11d, the property of her mistress Mrs. Mary Walker, of Bellwood Farm, Halton. Prisoner who appeared in dourt in an hysterical condition was accommodated with a seat in the dock.—Mra. Mary Walker said she was the wife of Mr. Gilbert Walker, of Bellwood Farm, Halton. Prisoner had been in her em- ploy for about a week as a domestic servant. She came to her from Lomas' a neighbouring farm. She identified the articles produced as hers. Witness had spoken to the girl about the things being missing, but she denied all knowlf dge of them. Information was given to P.C. Juett, who also charged her with the offence but she said she did not do it. She saw the things safe only a few days before they were misied.The corset was in a drawer in her bedroom, but she could not tell exac:ly where the ring was.—Martha Fletcher, a single woman, resid- ing at Frodsham Bridge, stated that the prisoner came to see her on Sunday last in the afternoon. She asked witness if he would change the corsets with ber as hers did not fit- She did so. Prisoner also made her a pre- sent of the riog.—By the Superintendent of the Pollee : Prisoner first asked her if she would buy the ring. She replied she bad no use for it. It was afterwards that she gave it to witness. It was the first time she had any- thing brought to her.—Prisoner stated that this witness asked her to bring anything she could gct to her.—Wit- ness denied this.—Police Sergeant A. J. Bourne (Sutton) said he received information of the theft and from inquiries visited the previous witness from whom he received the corset, and was also told how she became possessed of it. Subsequently he got the ring from Samuel VVhithy, farm labourer of Park Side. Be charged the prisoner with the offence and brought her to the Police Station. She appeared all right, but got a little excited. —Joynson pleaded guilty and electing to he summarily dealt with, was bound over in bee own and her mother's recognisance of 40s each to keep the peace for 6 months. —Pr_secutor did not prARq

ANNUAL MEETING AT THE Y.M.C.A. ROOMS. In the Leann Hall, at the YMC A Rooms, on Sun- day afternoon, the anti annual meeting of the P.S.A. Society in connection with the institution was held. Mr. Henry Taylor (vice-president), presided, and spoke of the advantages of the P.S.A. movement. Mr. Wicidle gave a short address on " Moral Courage," and Messrs. Atherton and F. Hickman also took part in the meeting. A special prize was awarded to Mr. Thomas Barber, a member of the society, for his zeal during the year in bringing new members to the meeting. Mr. W. CLEGG, secretary, read his annual report, which was as follows :—" In my last report I stated that our society had had a very successful and prosperous year, and, in fact we ventured to call it a record year.' We commenced 1898 in the full hope of maintaining that high standard of excellence, scarcely expecting to out- strip our previous attainments. We have, however, made some progres2, and the year 1898 stands foremost in the history of our movement. We commenced with 184 members on the register, and have closed with 292, One hundred and eight of these have ceased to attend, which loaves a balance of 184 for the new register, or the same as last year. Of the 108 our visiting committee give a very satisfactory account. Sunday labour, left town, change of circumstances, indisposition, and kin- dred reasons account for a great many, whilst it gives us pleasure to state that others have commenced active service in the Sunday schools of our town, one as super- inteadent, two as secretaries, others as teachers and scholars. Toe total number of attendances made at our own premises is 5.939, which gives an average of 124 at each meeting, as against 117 of last year, being, an average gain of seven at each meeting. Toe qu- r- terly prize book system has again ben very popular,and it is encouraging to note that the books asked for have been more than usual of an educational character—re-

ligione, social, and scientific bo3ks, era prominent amongst our quarterly prizes. Prayer Woks, hymn books, and Bibles have also been supplied. The total number of b)oks given is 496, . as against 511 last year, or a decrease ot 15. Tnis is accsunted for by the more systematic way in which the marking is being done. We tender to our atsentee visitors our Ivarty thanks for the manner in which they have done their work, the re- sults, as stated_ previously, being very encouraging. The benevo'ent fund of our society is still doing its work quietly. A member of the committ.e in the early part ot the year provided a b3x to be placed at the door, and I am pleased to state that the receipts from that source have exceeded the demands made. The general funds of the society still remain in a satisfactory con- dition, which reflects great credit to cur treasurer, Mr. Helford. Great praise is due to the Musical Commit- tee for the excellent talent they have invited here. Our best thank; are also due to the ladies and gentle- men who have done so much te make the musical portion of our services bright. In pro- viding chairmen for our meetings our thanks are due to Mr W U Hurst, and Mr %V Roberts. We very much appreciate their efforts. Our Preildeat (Mr. Hickman), has provided speakers, and our hearty thanks are due to him. The services throughout the year have ben of a spiritual and he p'ul character. Before conch' ling I would name for special Chalks Mr Gregson for his services as acting vice-president, Mr Wools as representing the Musical Committee, Mr E S Tayler and Mr W E Roberts as markers; Mr F Rickman, Mr G B Holford, and Mr Atherton for presid- ing at the piano and -ran; Messrs Barnes, E Taylor, J Whitmore, W Wood, a H Heaford and Gregson, the Visiting Committee, and to all who had in any way contributed to the success of our work. Tne election of officers and committee took place last Sunday, and resulted as follows :—President, Mr William Hickman ; acting vice-president, Mr Henry Taylor; treasurer, Mr George Holford ; secretary Mr William Clegg • committee, Mrssrs W Woods, E Hickman, W Ma' ikin, E Barnes, E Taylor, J Whit- mere, W Atherton, W Rabarts, 11 Clough, T Barber,. Themes Garnett, W Gregson, J Worthington, J Ryder, Thomas Massey, H Pluinpton, Heaford, and R Wood. The motto of the year, Stand fast in the faith,' we trust has been a source of strength and help to the mem- bers and thus served its purpose." (Applause.) The report was adopted. -

div.head: A. SERIES OF Pat THEFTS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: A. SERIES OF Pat THEFTS AT WARRINGTON.

At .the Warrington Borough Police Court on Thursday morning, before Mr. John Pairclough (chairman), Alder- man Sutton and Mr. J. Hepherd, several cases of thefts, were heard.—Thomas Brown, a stranger to War- rington, pleaded guilty t 3 s:ealing a gentleman's woo len sweater and two pairs of ladies stockings, altogether value lie 6i. from a shop in Sankey street on Wednes- day afternoon, the property of William Rhodes, stock buyer, Win wick-road. The Chief Constable said that at 12-25 on Wednesday afternoeo,Detectivas Meaceck and Delahry saw prisoner wandering about the market, and pricing things at different stalls. Their suspicions caused them to watch him, and they followed him to Sankey-street, and he went into complainant's snop where the sale was pro- ceeding arid picked up the articles. When he came out of the chop the officers saw that his coat was bulging out, and they followed him into a barber's shop, where prisoner had plac d the sweater o": a chair. The officers searched him, and found the stockings on him. The ankles were identified, an I prison, r was taken into custody. He looked an old hand at that sort of game. The magistrates sent priAmer to gaol for one month's hard labour. Two litt;e girls, named Ellen and Alice Smith, resid- ing with their parents at 36, Rolleston-street, were next eearged with stealing from Messrs. Peacock Bros.. stall in the Market Hall on Sa•urday night a large number of small articles, including three handkerchiefs, seven spoons, a salmon tin op mer, laces, and beads valued at is 61. Tney pleaded guilty. The Caret Constable said the case might seem at first sight a trivial one, but he hcl been assured by Mr. Peacock, sen., who had several stalls in the market, that they were at a considerable annual loss through little pilferers, and they must make an example of someone. Thee kept a penny stall, and were daily pestered by children, and it sometimes tre k four or five people to watch the stall. At about 7.30 on Saturday night the defendants went to Peacock's stall with a bag, evidently prepared for their enterprise, ad they were watched, beug known as little thieves. The youngest girl took the articles whilst her sister, who had the nag " covered her," a 3 it was describcd.—Defendants were each fined ss. The last case heard was that against William Fitz- gerald. described as a travelling thief,who was charged with ,tealing from Mr. Unsworth's shop, Lyme-street, or, Wednerday afternoon, five caps, valued at 2s 8-Id. He pleaded guilty aiel said he did it "for a lark" and that lie was drunk.—The Chief Constable said at 3-45 on Wednesday afternoon prisoner went in Unswcath's shop and offered a ring representing it as, gold for sale, but Mr. Shaw, who was in the shop, was not "green," and told prisoner to go. He left the shop, and was noticed to pick up the caps as he did so and conceal them about his pErs m. Mr. Shaw followed him and gave informa- tion to P.S. Lewis, vela) apprehended prisoner in Rutter- market-street. Prisoner was what they called"a travel- ling thief." Peisaner who had previously been convicted was sent to gaol with hard labour for three months.

LATEST NEWS. FIGHTING IN UGANDA. A BRITISH FORCE AMBUSHED. THIRTEEN KILLED. ZANZIBAR, DECEMBER 14. In English traveller from Ugauda Drings news that Lieut. Hannynton of the 27th Bombay Infantry, and a detachment of his men, fell into an ambuscade laid for them by the Soudanese mutineers at Kisaliza, towards, the beginning of October. The mutineers, who have been hiding near Lake Kioga, afcer being defeated by the British force, crossed the lake at night, and taking Lieut. Hannynton's party by surprise forced them to beat a retnat with a loss of thirteen men killed and wounded. Lieut. Hannynton was weunde.d in two places, and the rebels succeeded in capturing fifteen hundred Martini cartridges. It is believed that their chief object was to obtain the supply of ammunition. FOOTBALL. HAYDOCK V. SKERTON. (LANCASHIRE JUNIOR CUP). This replayed Junior Cup Tie was played at Haydock yesterday afternoon, during a hurricane that blew off the top of the grand stand and carried away part of the hoardings rcund the field. In the first half Skerton, as. slated by the wind, scored two goals. In the second half Greene!' headed through for Haydock. The home team had very hard lines during tuis hill, hut were unable to draw level. Final :—Skerton 2 goals, Haydeck 1.

div.p: SHOCKING TRAGEDY IS BEDFORD-
SHIRE. MURDER AND SUICIDE BY A LODGER.

Bletchley correspondent telegraphs :—Ye-iterday morning, at Woburn Sands, a village in Bedfordshire, a drayman named George Jeffrey, who bad been lodging with a Mr. and Mrs. Burt, enterEd Mrs. Burt's bedroom after her husband had left for work anl cut her throat, and then fatally cut his own throat. There was no alga of a struggle, and no motive is alleged for the crime. A PASSENGER STEAMER ON FIRE.

Lloyd's agent at Alicante teiegraphs :—The Italian steamer Vittoria. bound from Genoa for Buenos Ayres with a cargo of general goods' arrived with her cargo on fire, which is still burnisg. Tne sulphur is on fire, and preparations are being made for scut:ling the vessel. The number of passengers on board is stated to be 400 emigrants. The passengers are being landed. WRECK OF A CARDIFF STEAMER.
MADRID, THURSDAY. The crew of the British steamer Rhyrnoey, 1,300 tons, of Cardiff, were nafely lauded yesterday after the loss of their vessel in the Gulf of Viscaya.

LIEUTENANT WARK.

REMOVAL OF THE PRISONER FROM LIVERPOOL. Lieutenant Wark was removed from Walton Gaol yesterday en route for her Majesty's Prison at Stafford. He was brought down quietly from Walton in a convey- ance, and taken to one of the Liverpool railway stations. He appeared to be fairly well in health, and was not very much dejected. II!, was recognised by some friends who were on the look out for his removal, and in reply t 3 a wish that he might keep his bean; up, he replied : "This last blow has done for me." He proceeded to say he did na know 11.3 w to thank sufficiently the Liverpool pi.ople for their kindness. But he would thank them heartily, and he desired espeeially to be re- membered to some individials whom he mentioned. The ex-lieutcnaut was handcuffed to the youth from Blackpool, recently sentenced to a term of penal servi- tude for embezzlement.
