div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.
A RIXTON FARMER CHARGED WITH ASSAULTING A POLICE INSPECTOR.

At the Warringtcn Borough Police Court on Monday merning, before Mr. F. Monks (in the chair) and other magistrates, William Mawdsley. farmer, Rixton, was charged With being drunk in charge ot a horse and lorry in Bridge-street, at one p.m. on Saturday. He was also charged with assaulting Inspector Taylor at the same time and place,and doing damage to his macintesh to the amount of is. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defendant. —lnspector Taylor said at the time named he was near the Feathers dotal when he saw the defendant in charge of a horse and lorry. He was driving at a 'furious rate in the direction of Bridge-foot. He shouted to him to stop,but he took no notice of him, and witness -rushed to the furry and clung to it, as he was deter- mined to stop such furious driving. The defendant ad- dressing the horse, kept on saying go on Bonny, go on Bonny." while the wife remarked "Go on, never mind him '5 (the officer). P.C. Gibbe was in the street at the time, and be assisted witness. The defendant was very excited and the horse got so but witness stuck to its head, and eventually they got the defendant out of the lorry, but he was no sooner on his feet than he struck witness several times in the chest, mouth and eyes. Defendant. I don't remember that.— Continuing, Inspector Taylor said the defendant was very drunk and violent, and did all he could to upset witness and Gibbs while taking him to the Police Station. Be refused to t3O searched, and was with difficulty taken to the cells.—William Russell, cab and coach pro- prietor, said he was in the street at the time, and the defendint was driving as a terrific rate.—Witness saw him strike the Inspector.—Robert Smith, grocer and vision dealer, corroborated.—Mr. Browne said the defen- dant's relatives had instructed him to appear, but after the evidence which had been given it would be useless to attempt to deny the charges. He was hewever a respectable farmer. The defendant had been in town all day without food, and he admitted that he bad bad too much drinx.—Defendant was fined 5s and costs for beirg drunk, 10s and costi for furious driving, and ordered to pay is tor damaging the officer's macintosh—altogether RI. 14s 6d. FURIOUS DRIVING BY A FARMER.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. Monks , (in the chair) and other magis- trates, Mr. John Marsh. a well-known farmer, of Brad- ley Ball Farm. Grappenhall, was charged with furiously driving a horse aol trap in Kuutsford-ro Li to the dan- ger of passengers on the 31st Decernb-r, at 11 20 p.m.— Defendant pleaded not guilty.—Sergeant Smith said P.C. Pennington was with him on the night in question, and they were standing near a gas lamp. The defend- ant drove past at the:rate of 14 miles an hour. There was a man in the trap with him. He recognized Mr. Marsh.—P.C. Reddington corroborated. —Richard Get- non, 'bus driver for Mr. Connor, said he was in charge of a 'bus in Knutsford-road on the night in question when the defendant passed him in his trap. Ha was going at the rate of 14 miles an hour.—Defendant: I am surprised that such answers should be given.—Mr Frank Kerfoot said the defendant had offered to drive him home on the night in question, and he accepted the offer. The animal made a spring when passing the 'bus, but pulled up immediately afterwards. In his opinion, there was neither furious nor reckless driving. Be would not tell a lie, even to please Mr. Marsh, aud if he thought he was driving furiously he would have given evidence against laim.—Defenaant was fined 53. including costs.
OMNIBUS R WING ON KNIITSFORD-ROAD.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. Monks (chairman), and ether magistrates. Joseph Burrows, 'bus driver, 15, Bridgewat?r-3treet,and Robert Cleminson, 48, Knutsford-road, were charged with furiously driving 'buses in Knutsford-road, on the 3rd January.—Defendants pleaded not guilty.--The Chief Constable said the defendants were drivers, one for Mr. Connor, the other for the Carriage Company. He had received numerous complaints from the public about the inconvenience and danger caused by 'busmen racing each other for passengers, and if this case was proved he would ask the Bench to inflict a severe penalty. They endeavoured to pass each other on the road to get first on the stand.—The Chairman : Are the 'buses licensed ?—The Chief Constable replied that they were, but that the Watch Committee had no power to place any limitation on the time kept so long as there was no obstruction. He was pleased to say, irawever, that the Corporation were applying for Parliamentary powers to regulate the time tables for 'bus drivers.—P.C. Corcoran said the offence was committed at 7.30 in the evening. The defendants passed each other three times from the " Cheshire Cheese "to the Swing Bridge.—John Board- man said the horses were proceeding at the rate of nine miles an hour.—The Chairman commented on the serious nature ,of the offence, and fined defendants 103 each and costs. If, said Mr. Monks, there was any more of this nonsense the fine would be 403., or probably there would be a committal to prison without the option of a

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARUINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Parnay.—Before Dr. Cornell (chairman), Councillor Smethurst and Mr. James Hepherd. CHARGE or BREAKING A WINDOW. -John Foy was charged With being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street at 10-30 the previous night; and also with committing damage to a window to the amount of 2s. Prisoner pleaded guilty to the first offence and not guilty to the second. —P.C. Clough said he was called into the Brit. taunts Inn on the night in question and found prisoner in the custody of Mr. Finch, son-in-law of the licensee. Prisoner .WaS very drunk and used most filthy language and when taken into custody was very violent.—John Finch said the prisoner had been struggling with a woman outside the house and the window was broken between them.—The bench fined prisoner 108 and costs for the first offence and dis- missed the other charge, A CASE DISMISSED.---John Holbrook, Earle-street. was charged with assaulting Bertram Miller, 63, Orford-lane, on the 21st December.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defend- ant and Mr. F. R. Roberts represented the complainant.' Mr. Roberts said the complainant in the case was a WY of about 10 years of age. On the night in question the by had ocoasion to pass the shop of Holbrook's mother. As he passed some boys ran away and the defendant rushed oat of the shop and caught complainant, thinking him to be one of the defendants, and boxed his ears. The boy had suffered from a complaint of the ears for some time, and it caused the disease to break forth afresh. If his client had been one of the offending boys the defendant had no right to.take the law into his own hands.—The boy. Bertram Miller, bore out his solicitor's statement, and denied opening the door.— Other witnesses corroborated,—Mr. Browne said it was a very paltry case. The boy was playing with other boys when one of them opened the door of Holbrook's shop. A Mr. Stout, who was passing, held the boy knowing tha Mr. Holbrook was annoyed by the boys. When Mrt

Holbrook came he hit the lad once with his open hand.— James Stout. 16, Vere-street, said the complainant opened the door. Mr. Holbrook only hit him once.—Further evidence was given and the magistrates dismisse.i the ease Mexuay.- Before Mr. F. Monks (chairman), Aldermen Harrison and Blackhurst, Councillor Stiaw Green and Mr. Birchall,

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.-I'II9MTICe Hynes, a stranger to the town, was charged with this offense in Irlam-street on Saturday night. —Sergeant Hollingworth gave evidence.— The bench dismissed the case on his promise to leave the town.—ltichard Britain was fined 5s and costs for a similar offence, and Ellen Connor, who made her 59th appearance was sent to gaol for one month.—Richard Wilkins, Ellen Hughes, and Margaret Owen, were all fined 5s and costs for this offence _ _

ASSLULT ON THE PoLicm.—William Cotton was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket street on Saturday night and also with assaulting P.C. Carter whilst In the wcecution of his duty.—Defendant pleaded guilty.— PC. Carter said be was arresting a woman named Connor when he was struck a violent blow in the face over the front teeth by the defendant whom he had never seen before. The blow stunned him for a time.—Another officer corroborated. —The Chairman said interfering with the police was a seri- ous matter, and prisoner would have to go to gaol for a month.

QUARRELSOME WOMEN.—Bridget Conway and Annie Ross were charged with committing a breach of the peace on the Ist December. —Sergeant Williamson said on the day in question the defendants were fighting most desperately in Dial-street with their hands in each other's hair.—Ross : I have never been here before—The Chief Constable : Oh stop that You have been here 48 times before.—The bench bound them over in one surety each of £5 for six months and ordered them to pay the costs 7s each or in default• seven days. FOOTBALL IN THE STREETS--James Barker (17), 3 Edge- worth-street ; Harry Ince (15), 64 Legh-street) ; Albert Boardman (15). 60 Legh-street ; and Thomas Lawton (15), 41 Kendrick-street, were all summoned for playing football in Beamont-street on the 2nd January.—Defendants pleaded guilty.—Detective Roper proved the case. —The Chief Con- stable said he had received bitter letters of comolaint about it. It was a regular thing down there.—The magistrates final defendants Sc each. OBJECTORS TO VACCENATION.—Yhe Rev. James Thomas Schofield. pastor of the Baptist Chapel, Golborne4treet, and residing in Crosfield-street applied for an exemption eertifi- cats. Applicant said his child was born on the 30th Septem- ber, and he had conscientious objections He had suffered himself for years through being vaccinated. He believed the risk from the remedy was far worse than the disease. Alderman Harrison: It is a mere matter of opinion. You do not support that by a particle of evilence.—Applicant : I can explain but the law says that I have only to state my objections.—Alderman Harrison: I don't knew whether to take your word.—Applicant : I can make a fuller state- ment —The Bench granted the application.—Alfred Robin- sots, 73, Marsh House-lane also made application with respect to his child Dorothy. The Chairmaa : You will rue this some day.—Alderman Harrison: We shall have an epidemic of small pos.—Alderman B.ackhurst : We must grant the applications if they have conscientious objections.—A.der- Harrison : Not necessarily. They do not grant them in some places.—The application was granted.
TUE§DAY.—Before Mr. B. Garnett (chairman). Councillor Shaw Green and Ur. Birchall. . _

A ROUGH CUSTOMER.—John Patrick Mary was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road on the previous night and with assaulting P.C. Hesp. —The offic sr stated that prisoner was drunk and had his coat off challeng- ing the people round about to fight. Witness moved him on and he made filthy remarks and struck him twice in the teeth. Witness had a deal of trouble in getting him down to the police station.—The Bench committed him to gaol for 14 days' hard labnur. TRAVELLING WITHOUT PAYING PA s.—Matthew aohn Flynn and William Riley were charged with travelling on the L. and N.-W. Railway from Rainhill to Warrington with- out paying their fares.— Both prisoners pleaded guilty. - Detective Howell said the previous night the two defendants arrived at /lank Quay Station by a train due from itainhill at 9.20 p.m. A ticket collector namel Holland asked them for their tickets and both denied having been on the train, and said they had been to see a friend off from Birkenhead. Flynn pulled out 6d fram his pocket and tried to induce the collector to piss them througn the gate. Witness was sent for and Riley said " there will be a b—hot shop here directly." They were taken to the office where P.C. Leonard happened to be, and searched. One had Sid on him and the other sd. Prisoners then acknowledged coming from Rain- hill. Both were very rough on the way to the Mice Station. —P.C. Pennington said he had known the man Flynn for 12 years. He never did any work and the other man was an associate of Flynn's.—They were each tined 20s and costs or one months' imprisonment. AN APPLIOLTION Os EXEMPTION.—Peers Turner, 129, Forster-street,in making application sal .1 he had conscientious objections to vE.ccination, he thought vaccination spread disease.— The Chief Constable: We shall hava a high old time at the next epidemic of small-pos.—Mr. Birckall : We have simply got to carry out the provisions of the Act.—The Chairman : Have you had toy experience of what you say. —Applicant: No sir.—The abplieation was granted. WEDNESDAY. --Before Mr. James Fairclough (chairman), and
Messrs. Geddes and Birefiall.

"WOULD HAVE TO STELL."—John Coult was charged with stealing a piece of bacon value 6s 6d the previous day.— Prisoner pleaded guilty.— The Chief Constable said about 4.33 the previous day prisoner went into the shop of Messrs. Povey and Duckworth, Buttermarket-street, and begged of the assistant James William Warburton. He was refused and lett the shop muttering he would have to steal. Shortly after a piece of bacon was missed from the customers' side of the counter. Superintendent Monaghan later saw prisoner going into shop). His pocket seemed bulky, ani he took him down to the poll m station. The man was not stealing from need as he bad Is 81:1 on him. 149 was tinder the in. fluence of drink.---The bench committed him to prison for one month with hard labour.

THURWAY.—Before Mr. T. J. Gillespie (chairman) and Messrs. Robert Stone, Mid T. D. Grim'i6 Drayton. MINoR CASES.— The following were fine i for being drunk and disorderly :—James Bailey 5s and costs; Thomas Ley- land; 2s 6d ; and Thomas Travis, 51 and costs. Saraki Wore- ley for being drunk on December 31st was fined 2s 61 and costs, and Thomas B m.sr for an unlighted vehicle on Decem- ber 30th was fined 2s 6d and costs. Lewis Beresford was lined 108 and costs for being drunk in charge of a horse and trap nn Desember 23th and a fine of 5s and costs was inflicted upon William Chadwick for not having scales on his coal lorry on December 31st. A PROMISE TO S ON THE PLEDGE.—Wilfred Mat'aer was charged with persistent cruelty towards his wife Bather Mather. Mr. Riley for the defence pleaded no; guilty.—Complainaut said last week her hus- band asked her for money saying "It is &tiler a Knife or money." She did not like giving him money as he would only get tarink.—By Mr. Riley: He was a reasonable man except when he gave way to drink. He had not done any actual violence to her but she was afraid of what he would do.—Mr. Riley said the man was not tech- niePlly guilty and ha had promised not to take drink again. —The bench dismissed the case after getting a promise train the defendant that hiif would sign the pledge. UnsusT Scauxs.—Bleanor Wardall of Wigan was sum- moned for having unjust scales on•the 6th January.—ln- spector tthepherd said he rhited the defendent who was a greengrocer on the day in question about 7.33 and found the scales were 1 oz against the purchaser. A ring was Off the scales which would make the differenne.—Defendant said she was not aware the ring had fallen off them.—The magis- trates paid they were inclined to believe her statement and fined her 2s 6d and costs. FAULT:JO TO DELIVER A PIG LICENSE —Matthew Lowe was charged with failing to deliver to the police a reinovai license for pigs.—lividence Was given us support a. the case.— SuaErintendeut Brassington said the license allowed four days' grace before being delivered.—The Chairman said see- ing he had been so long in the trade he must have known perfectly well what to do and fined him 10a and costs.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
MONDlT.—Befora Messrs. Clnries Reynolds (presiding), and
F. J. Norman:

CONTRAVENTToN OF TIIE SHOP HOURS REGULATIONS.— George C. Duckett, fiehmonger, Regent-street. was summoned by William Dunlop Laird, inspector under the Shop Hours Regulation Act, 1892. that he on the 17th December, em- ployed a young person named John Edward James in his shop contrary to the provisions of the Act.—Defendant pleaded not guilty.—luspecter Laird said the action was taken under &lotion 4 of the Shop Hours Regulation Act, 189?, which provided that no young person should be em- ployed for longer than 74 hours a week; and also that in shops where young persons were employed a notice stating the hours during which such person should be employed should be posted up. By " young person" the Act meant anyone under the age of 13 years. The defendant had offended in both these provisions. —Albert Timmins stated he was an inspector under the Act,and on the 17th of December last at a wieder past eleven on Saturday night he called at defendant's shop. There were two boys working there, the boy John Edward James, and another named Basnett. He asked James what his hours of employment were and he said he worked from eight to nine at night. Witness than went into the shop and spoke to the defendant about the poy. The regulation notice was nowhere to be seen ; a fact he called the delendant'a attention to. He had visited the shoppn a former occasion' when he cautioned the defendant's wife; The nature of the boys work was "calling fish and handing rabbits in." Defendant stated th at the boy was employed by h:m and lived in the house.— Thomas Wright said he was an assistant-inspector. He was with ter. Timmins on the occasion of his visit to the defena- ant's shop a• d could corroborate.—Defendant stated he was entirely innocent of offending against the Act. He had the notice put up and it remained there until the painters came in.No doubt it was then taken down and he had forgotten all about it. The boy he employed was a Liverpool la-4. He did not employ him over the stipulated time, as the lad got Weduesday afternoon, and a part of Saturday to himself, Staying on the Saturday night in return.—The boy was in Court and on being called etated ho had seen the notice on the wall in the shop, and it was there until the paperhangers came in a few weeks ago After the inspector had been an- other was procured and put up. Ho seemed perfectly satis- fied with his place.—lnspector Laird said it was not a very serious ease, but as it was the first in the district under that Act, he wanted it to be as a warning to employers.—The Chairman said that being so they would deal leniently with he case, but shopkeepers who offended in future would be everely dealt with.—A. fine of is end costs Was imposed. AFTER Meer DAYS.—Joseph Hopley, late of Okell-street, Runcorn, was apprehended on warrant charged with using obscene language in Greenway-road, on the 22nd of August last.—He pleaded guilty, stating the reason he had not appeared before was because he did not like to.—P. C. Gill proved the case.—Hopley salt he now lived in Fern- worth.—Fined 5s and costs, or 14 days. DIEGLECV AND HIPOSURE OF AN INFANT IN ARMS. MOTREIS SENT TO Pat3on.—Ann Corcoran, a woman who of late has been several times before the court, was brought up in custody charged with wilfully exposing her child Ann Corcoran, aged 18 months, in such a manner a 3 to be likety to cause suffering to its health. on the 7th of January.— Prisoner pleaded guilty. —P.O. J. Smith. stated two about 9 p.m on the day in question he saw the prisoner very drunk in Bridge-street. She had a child in her arms, very mach exposed. She was very drank and !ell to the floor several times to the danger of th 3 infant It was a wet and damp Carrington testified to having to caution the prisoner earlier in the day.—The prisoner said she had no in- tention of exposing the child, it was in consequence oF the drink Bios had had. —The Chairman : You will be committed tolinutsford for 4 calendar mouths with hard labour.

Simister went full back. Half-tims score:— Widnes, one try ; Stockport, nothing. Jobne restar;ed Bellamy returning, and St6ckport ct into the visitors' half. Robinson got possession, but was immediately in Mar- tin's arias. Wi Ina; war.! penalised. and S aviVe mtde a bil for goal. from half.way, but the ball fell under the crossbar. Loose play followed, and then Stockport caused their opponents some anxiety, but Baty got a leek in just in time.and Whines forced their way to the home line, whore B ttey got 'possession and ranning through scored, the same player placing a goal. Widnes were soon presAng again, but Sands saved. Stockport were given a trce kilk, and play ' was in the visitors' quart its. Taylor relieved, and Robinson, tikiag a pass from Wo!sley, made a good run, but still no score came. Oa the other hand, Widnes again got up, and Rispan dropped 'a goal.Result:—Widnes,two goals and two tries (ten points) ; Stockport nil. _ Sr. HELENS v. SALFORD.

At St. Helens. An attempt to get the Salford backs on the rum was thwarted, and from a tnee kick by Foulkes, Briers got away and nearly scorel. Stott was next tackled near the line. A fine run was made by Griffiths and Pea-son, but Sidd all saved. Griffislas sub- sequently dropped a beautiful goal for Salford. The visitors had several free kicks at the centre, but they came to nothirre, and then St. Helens broke away again. A free kick Wing granted to St. Helens, Foulkes just missed kieking a goal. A moment later he missed anether goal from a splendid drop after a pass from Little. S. Helens had rather the best of the play, but a mark by Browne led t 3 Salford coming to half-way. Williems and Sharpe made a grand run down the field, but Foulkes seeured the ball and kicked to the centre. St. Helens curtinued to have the best of matters, but could not break through. Stott was next to attempt a drop, but failed. Salford then took up the attack, and a splendid passing run by Crocker, T. Williams, and Sharpe ended in the latter scoring a good try. Griffiths failed at goal. St. Helens again got on their opponeats' line, but the ball was xicely worked out of Aaager. Liverzage received at centre, and made a grand run to the Salford liar, but was tackled. Stott, however, snored a brilliant try, F3ulkes tailing at goal. Interval ' score : Salford: one goal and one try ;S. Helens one tr 7. Williams in- tercepted a pass by Stott and gave to Crocker, who was well tackled. Griffiths kicked up the field strongly, and Foulkes retuned. Salford then had matters in their favo ir, but were met with a capital defence by the home backs. St. Helens were pressed, but the forwards broke away wi-h a splendid ran into too Salford half. Whiteley restarted for Sc. Helens. and Salford at once bseame dangerous, but a good kick by Little brought the ball t) the centre. St. Helens attempted to get their three-quarters going, but the Safford backs entered the horns half, when passing between Gray, Sharpe, and Gledhill resulted in the latter scoring, T. Williams failing to place a gee'. The Salford backs a'terwards got pm- session, ana a quick run r3sulted in the ball being sent over the home line and kicket deal twice in succession. Liversage was in turn prominent for St. Helene, but was brought down after a good run into the Stlford half Siddall later gained a try for St. Helene, and Foulkes kick.d a goal. Result :—St Helens, one goal and two tries (eight points) ; Salford, one goat and two tries (eight points). OLDHAM v. MORECAMBE.

The Moreetmbe fifteen were no match for Oldham, who were playing at horns. Fletcher. Lees, Martin and Davies were among the scorers for Oldham, wh3 won by three goals and seven tries to nil. This match, at Leeds. was spoiled by a heavy mist, and the game had to be stopped before the appointed time. Nothing was scored, and the match, such as it was, ended in a draw.

BRADFORD v. BRIGHOUSE RANGERS. The Rangers, playing on the Bradford ground, gained a well-merited win by two goals and one try to one try. Naylor kicked a penalty goal for the wineers and Ross scored a try, Cooper was the try-getter for Bradford.

Halifax we:a der-i3ively beaten at Liversedge by three goals and three tries to nil. Wallace drooped a goal, while Todkill, Davidson, and Jenkinson obtlined trier. HUDDERSFIELD V. WAKEFIELD TRINITY.
The foggy weather at Huddersfield grfatly • irt4ferel with the plly. Neither side could score, and the result was a draw.

WARRINGTON " A " V. PICK OF JUNIOR LEAGUE. This match which was brou 'tit off on Saturday, was promoted with a view to assisting the newly formed Junior League. The proceeds are to be set apart by the Warrington committee for the benefit of the Lague fund. There was a" gate "of about 3,000 spectators. The teams were composed as follows :—Junior League : Morgan, full back ; Knight, Hockenhull, Lowe, and Campbell, three-quarters ; Kidd and Armitage, half- backs ; Bramall, Foden, Roylance, Ditchfiald, Bibby, Bromley, and Lythgoe. forwards. Warrington : Bos- cow, lull baca ; Pendlebury, Ratcliffe, Moores, Nelson, three-quarters ; R Bate, and Hill, half-backs ; Cunning- ham, Wilcox, Sefton, Skelhorn, Dakin, Eden, Hatton, Barratt, forwards. Dakin kickel off for Warrington, the homesters immediately pre,ssinze Moores scored within a few minutes and improved with a goal kick. Even play followed for some time, Boscovv playing a re- liab!e game. Ratcliffe then got over the line, Moores this time failing to make the ball rise. The superior tactics of the borne players were apparent the visitors being kept on the defence, Hill being instrumental in scoring another try, Ratcliffe adding two more points. The visiting forwards broke away on the restart, p lasing well along the line, Pendle- bury finally intercepting. The check was only momen- tary however ;play being transferred to the pavilion end at the corner, the soared defence of the homestere keeping their liae intact. The vi•iters were out-played and play taken to the opposite end where the "juniors" had to kick dead. Later, Hill got over and the score at half-time i'ies 16 points to nil in favour of Narrington. The visitors had the advantage of play early in the second half, and were only checked on the line. They gained a free kick which was a good attempt. War- rington pressed and after a splendid run Eden grounded at the corner. The leek for goal was a wild one. The vi,itors forced play into the Warrington quar- t-re, Hughes making a useful mark. Erchange kicking of which the visitors had the best took play in front of the home goal where through their lack of finish the "Juniors "missed an opportunity. Play waa of a scram- bling nature aft-r this, Moores again crossing the line in grand style,Ratcliffe's kick for goal striking the upright. When time arrived the visitors were pressing, the score being Warrington 22 points, Junior League nil.

The Chairman said th y met Mr. Raiford who in- formed them that with a certain amount of money to assist thern the County Councl would readily asst the people of Great Sankey. Mr. Radford said it was quite necessary there should be an alteration ia the bri ige. He felt sure in his own mind the', when they ware prepared to move in the matter and th hid th 3 favour able views of the railway company,the County Council would as ;ist them.

Mr. Thompson : The opinion 19 that thil Parish Coun- cil should get plans and the probable cost of the under- taking. The Chairman: We are entirely in the hands of the London and North-Virestern Railway company. Th,. Clerk: In any case the County C.nricil will not contribute nalre than one third of the cost,so that it will leave a very big sum to becontributed by somaone else. The Chairman: The District,* Council might con- tribute.

- The Chairman said, as a member of the HighwaV Board, some two months ago plans were submitted to the members of that body of an extensive scheme to straighten the highway road from Sankey to Warring- ton. Oa seeing those plans he thought it woilld be a wonderful improvement. The read wild be cenverted from Penketh-lane end in a straight liae—if agreeable to the landowners in the immediate proximity—across Buttermilk Bridge and elms out at Sankey Lodge Hall corner of Lwely-lane, and direct to the fo ,t of B talc Quay Bridge. The Surveyor of toe Highway Board was busily engaged in coming to terms with the landowners and if settled it woull be a facility both for the traffic and tne landowners in the vicinity. WARRINGTON WIN AT WIGAN.

The first match of the N-/w Year ended irt,;st satisfac- torily for Warrington on Saturday, and was thus in decided contrast to the same erelt a year ago when. Leigh swamped the Warringtoniani at Leigh. Wigaa were the opponents this time, anl having choice of grounds it was expect ,d that they would prove f amid- ahle opponents, even thin el they wore well beaten at Warrington. Tne vieitor, too, had to mike the journey wichnit their captain, Smack Be., and were thus serioualy haadicappd. Duckworth filled the vacancy, Allen also travelling to Wigan in Case Duck worth had not turned up. Wigan were :eprosented by their best team. The weather was very suitable for the game, and the ground, though heavy, not in bad order. About 1,590 spee.tators watched the encounter, which was under the control of Mr. J. Priestley (Broughton.) The teams were as fellow& :

Warrington : Hallam, full back; Fish, Crcss, Isher- wood, and Harris, three-qu%rsers ; Ashurst, and Duck- worth, half-back a ; Navlor,fhardman' Taybr, Fairhurlt Sullow, Swift, Slholtze, and Towneni, forwards. Winn: John VVinatanley, fAll back; Catterly, Ball, Lewis, and Saunders, three-qulrters ; Dixon and Robin- son, half-hacks ; Yates, Prescott. Joe Winstanley, Pest, Rigby, Turner, Blackburn, and Bruwo, forwards.

Wirringt -keit the toss an i ;Taylor started against a light wind, a good return being made by Wiears. Isher- wood responded effectively, and the ho nesters had at once to defend. Warrington obteined pos:eseion from the first /scrimmage. and Ashurst throw across to Fish, who gathered the hell anti rounds-1 the Wigan threequarters in fine style, Whist anley finally checking him in the corner. A pant by Dixon momentarily re- lieved the prssure on the Wigan line, but Harris v- earned the attack with a dashing run down touch. Blackburn got aw ay with a useful dribble te Hallam, who proved safe, but carried the ball in touch. Toe kick-out by Robiuson sent Warrington te the right- about. Dixon secured and gave f.lttterly a nice pass, which the latter made very poor use of, Fish upsetti sg him promptly. Ashurst was instrumental in taking play back to the Wigan end. A. clever conebin,d move- ment by the Warrington backs gained further grouad. Both sides glaved with great determination, hut there was more dash in the Warr:neton front rank than in Wigan's, and a grand rush which took play near the home line mini injury to Peet: He was able to con- tinue playing however, Robiason played a sound defensive game, and on several occasions spoiled the tactics of the Warrington halves. A. short kick by Dixon almest caught H al- lam napping, but the visiting full back succeeded in securing the ball in time. Townend followed up well and charging Winstanley's kick down had the line at his mercy when ha was obstructed. Even play followed for a spell, but the aup,riority of the Warrington bac,e3 made itself felt. Harris twice made good attempts to get through but was well tackled. Isher wood punted judiciously, and following up at top speed he grassed Peet near the home line. Warringtoe pressed at all points, and _Cross varying the attack by a drop at goal, had hard luek to hit the upright. Fa-am the next pack Ashurst passed smartly to Isherwoed who ran in smartly and scored. Hellarn male a good attempt at goal. Ashurst and Fish made a further promising movement which was checked, and then Wive' dashed down to the other end. Hallam picked up and making a megnifieeet dodgy run punted into the home half, a p,eee•of play that was deservedly applauded. Just on half time Hal- lam was penalised for what looked like a knock for ward to Isherweed, and John Winstaniey tried, at only to fail by a yard or two. The interval arrived with Warring- t)n leading by a try to nil. Brown resumed hostilities and Warrington quickly returned to the attack. Smart passing by Ashurst. Isherwood, and Harris saw the latter race over, Win- stanley shoring him in teach at the corner. Warm work on the line tanked omnoue for Wiesn,and &shunt passed out, bat Ball averted the danger by a safe tackle of Isherwood. Gembined ferwerd play by the homesters drove Warriagtors back, Hallam bAnl tackled in his own half. A short punt to Winstanlev caught ‘th s lat- ter a little out of plec., and the usu illy safo full back mulling at centre, Fish came up at top speed and taking the ball on the bounce gained a fine try beneath the posts. The scorer was quite unopposed,and walked the last tea yards. Isherwood toik the goal-kick and added a couple more points. Wigan were in a bad Way now, and only just succeeded in keeping Fish out. Dixon was slow and enabled Boardm sn to pounce upon him near the line, a proceeding which caused the Wigan half- back to limp for the rest of she game. Wigan were penalised and Hallam made a grand attempt from near touch, the ball hitting the cross-bar right in the centre and rebounding into play. Near the core Wigad made a final effort, and established themselves on the War- rington line. Ball and Catterly both teed to get through hut were well tackled. Prescott and It sleinsoa also dashed in only to be bowled over inside the rut. War- rington defended vigorously, and at last Duckworth eased the pressere with a flying kick to centre. The final arrived soon after, and Warrington retired winners of a well contested game by I goal 2 tries (8 points), to Wigan nil.

div.head: SWINTON v. RUNCORN.
div.p: SWINTON v. RUNCORN.

This return match was played at Swinton on Satur- day, before 3,000 spectators. No rain fell during ths afternoon, bat the ground was very heavy and the ball greasy, while a heavy mist hung around. The visitors came without Warder. Farmer, and Reece. who had missed the train, but able sub.ttutes in Tomlinson,Bet- ley. and Hai wood were found. Teams : Swinton : J G,)odman' full back; J Valentine (cap- tain), V Hampson, R J Messer, and J M Bevan, three- qqarter backs ; W Pearson, and F. Morgan, lralf backs' J Eva •s, J Worthington, C Holme, J Vickers, G Harris, R Tickle, J Reynolds, and J Johnson, forwards,

Runcorn : S Eloog,htoa (captain), full back; D Jonea, J Butterworth, S Hailwood, and T W•lkinson. three- quarter backs; J Jolley and J Faulkner, half backs ; S W Bettley, S Walker, A Taylor, T Darlington, 0 Hughes, J Tomlinson, W Li .11 tfoot. and F Gayter, forwards. Referee, Mr. W. M'Cutc heon, Oldham. Taylor kicked off for the visitors. Bevan returned, and Jolley making his mark, Runcorn attacked strongly. Valentine, Pearson, amt.] Bevan in turn relieved, but the visitors returned to the attack. mull by Houghton and a run betwe-n Moeser and Bevan took the ball to the visitors' quarter flag, but Jones and Butterworth made a beautiful combined run nearly the length of the field. Flampson anti Bevan made smart runs, hut both players were knock.,d into touch near the goal line. Then Good- man and Ltampsan had shots at goal, but minor points only resulted. Jolley and Hailwood, after scrummages close to the line, very nearly scored, but Valentine and Goodman defended stronaly. Swinton in turn attacked, but selfish play by Morgan lost an apparently good chance of scoring. The visitors after this had the best of the game but ends wore changed without either side having scored. Valentine restarted the game, and the Swintonians went off with a great rush, but Houghtoa, Jolley, and Butterworth saved toeir side by vigorous tackling. The visitors' forwards gained ground by short plasing, but Evans returned with a strong run, and was with difficulty held close to the Brie. After a couple of punts out to Swinton, Morgan,Messer, Valemine,and Hampson made a good run, which Hough- ton stopped. At length Bevan, from a smart pass by Morgan, scored a try for Swinton, and Goodman, from a place close to the touch line, kicked a goal. Upon re- suming, play for a time was at midfield. Then the Swinton forwards carried several packs, and Houghton was collared with the ball in his posees3ion on the goal line. Frce kicks to both sides led to no result. and Hampton had a chance, but was quickly floored b 7 Houghton. Gaodman saved a rush by the visitor's for- wards, an' Messer made a long punt, when Houghton got the ball over his own goal line, but instead of touch- ing down he ran it out, but was held a few yards from the line. The ball, after a scrummage, %sae passed out to Valentine, who dropped at goal, but it hit one of the posts and reboundel int) play. Goodman, however, picked it up and dropped a goal for Swinton. The home side continued to play up strongly,and several times ap- peared likely to break through, but their efforts lacked finish. Pearson, Goodman, and Hampson in turn tried dr-pa at goal, but minor points only resulted. Jolley, Buletworth, and Hailwood made a good run, but Geol- man collared the latter player when he was becoming dangerous. Swinton after this attacked strongly, but no further points were scored. Final score :—Two goals and one try (seven points) to nothing in favour of Swinton.

There have come under our immediate notice re- cently many cases similar to the one revealed in the fallowing letter, which we commend to your kiad consideration :

"May 2aci, 1898. "Dear Sirs,—Encicsed plaas3 find photo of my baby girl, aged thirteen months,which will no doubt interest you and parents having babies afflicted with that dreadful disease which the doctors term • marasmus' or wasting. Our little child was bora delicate, and from the first was unable to digest properly her natural food, i.e., mother's milk. The PO r little thing seemed doubled up with flatti- lency, and for week's we did not know what it was to have a night's rest. To make matters worse the milk failed, and we had to resort to cow's milk. This brought on consumption of the bowels, not through carelessness or improper feeding, for we were most careful, but from sheer weakness of digestive powers. Medical advice we had ; in fact, all was done ; beef juice tried. fresh as well as a patent preparaton of talf juiae, also a much advertised patent food, supposed to do won- ders. We gave each a fair trial. A friend b )thered me to try Scott's Emulsion, an idea which I ridi- culed at the time, feeling, certain that if a child could not digest one part milk and two parts water she could not digest heavy oil, and besides she was then nine months old, and almost skin and bone. Still I did try at first a teaspoonful, which was promptly rejected; then half, with same result ; then a quarter of a teaspoonful. This was retained, and we kept on. No ! the first bottle did not werk marvels as patent medicines are advertised to do, but it stopped the wasting and we were satis- fied. As the child grew stronger, we gradually in- creased the dose,till we got to the teaspoonful again. We:used seven bottles, and baby was fat and well in thres months. div.head: WIDNES AND THE LOStOCK PROFESSIONAL.
div.p: WIDNES AND THE LOStOCK PROFESSIONAL.

A meeting of the Investigation Committee was held in Manchester on Friday night, all the members being pre- sent. Mr. H. H. Waller, Brighouse Rangers, was in the chair. Widnes applied for the transfer of Ward from Lostock Gralam, on the ground that he was an amateur. Upon investigation It was found that Ward had signed a professional form for Lostock Gralam, but it was found that no proper agreement in writing between Ward and the Lostock Club had been made. The Com- mittee dnid, d that Ward was a professional attached to the Lostock Club, and severely censured that organiz3- tion for their faLlure to carry out profes3ional law 3, and also cen3ured Ward for misleading the Widnes Club, whilst a registercd professional of the Lostock Club.

div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
EARLETOWN v. TRAWDEN FOREST.

Earlestown met Trawden Forest on Saturday on the Earlestown ground in the first round proper of the Lan- cashire Junior Cup C >mpetition, b,fore about 1,500 spectators. Trawden Forest came with a pod repute- don, and they were considered favourites or the cup, but the result strewed that the prognostications for the defeat of th 3 home eleven were unfounded. Earlestown were short of Hampion, and had to play Hughes in his stead, but he was of very little use in centre. Trawdeu Forest won the toss, and chose to play up hill, Hughes kicking off. Earlstown immediately attacked, and within two or three minutes of the kick off Smith had an axe' llent opening, but he failed to take advantage of it. The pace was set at a terrific rate, and rapid visits were paid to each end ; play being about th 3 centre for some time, the half back defence of Earlestown was superb, Parr shiiaing repeatedly in the sterling work he put in. Finally the home team assumed the upper hand, and exerted some slight pressure. The right wing pair, Smith and Downes neatly worked down and Smith sent in a stinger which the goal-keeper cleared by cone, ding a corner. Trawden Forest got away to the top end, and Chew hai to run out to clear. Again the visitors got up and Durden sent in a swift low shot which Chew cleverly saved. Parr was a thorn in the visitors' Fide and frequently changed the venue of play. A series of fouls gave the visitors another oppor- tunity and a fruitless corner resulted. Eerlestown again got hold and some clever work landed them in their opponent; quarters. Hughes passed te Downs who banged the leather acres to the left and Settle outwit- ting the back, scored with a shot which gave the goal- keeper no chance, and this was the score at half time. On changing ends, the visitors having the advantage of the hill pressed somewhat, but they were unable to Feline a point. The pressure was at 7a3t relieved and Settle making a splendid run up the wing ended by sem.• lug a second point for the home team. The game was hotly contested to the finish, but Eerlestown managed to pass into the second round of the competition by 2 goals to n;1. NEW roN -LE-WILLOWS v. WHISTON RAMBLERS. div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

Sir,—The engraving of these buildings in your line Almanack for 1899, reminds me of a meeting of the Town Council on the fourth of October last at which the scheme was fully discuseed. The meeting was an unusually harmonious one, and all the mem- bers present agreed that a new and large police es- tablishment was needed to meet the requirements of the town. There was, however, a slight diverg- ence of opinion regarding the cost, some putting it at £16,000 and others at £30,000. This divergence elicited two remarkable statements which, I think, are worth being recalled even at this distant date. In order to allay the apprehensions of weak- kneed ratepayers as to the effect (if any) of the scheme upon the rates Mr. Alderman Roberts is re- ported to have said," that somehow or other, in spite of the large expenditure, each year, the rates did not go up." What a compliment was this to the conspicious ability and foresightedness of the finan- ciers of the Clrporation And must it not have fallen like balm upon the poorer class of taxpay3rs who feel the burden of six shillings in the pound already hanging about their necks ! In most places I presume, rates rise and fall with the exigencies of expenditure • but "somehow or other " this is not the case in Warrington. Perhaps our basis of sup- ply is so large and iso elastic that a little judicious tapping, here and there, is all that is needed to meet any extraordinary outlay. If there is any truth in this surmise, the ratepayers need not be alarmed at the new scheme of the 11.-,wn Council for raising the debt of the Borough to the sum of £998,000, equivalent to a charge of £l7, upon every man, woman, and child in Warrington! And then still further to comfort and strengthen the weak-kneed, Mr. Councillor Crosfield, referring to the cost of the new buildings,is reported to have remarked " that if they could get such a building for £16,000 it would be an ornament to the town and a very cheap building." As to the cheapness I can say nothing because I know nothing; but surely the councillor must have spoken inadvisedly with his lips when he applied the word "orna- ment" to a place for the detention and punishment of evil doers. Of course, Mr. Crosfiald has a per- fect right to his opieion, and so have I; and mine is that such an institution is a discredit rather than an ornament to any community, but especially to one so full of religioue appliances as Warrington is. Ilowever imposing the new structure may be it will stand before us as a saddening monument of the power of drink, and a grim mockery of the poverty and wretchedness within its walls.

In a little work recently published by Pearson Limited, the author, Mr. Horselev, a prison chap- lain of large experience, tells us that if the liquor traffic were stopped one police station and one prison would suffice for the whole of London. Would it not be wiser and more humane policy then for our councillors and magistrates to put forth their efforts to suppress the traffic instead of building a costly prison, and keeping a costly staff of officials to punish its unfortunate victims? Such a policy would merit and receive the gratitude of all who desire to see sobriety and order in our streets, and comfort in the homes of our working classes, who are now the greatest sufferers from the liquor trade. Prevention is always better than cure,ap.d never more so than in the case of drink.— Tours truly, - lONA.

div.head: CROOKING DEATH OF A WARRINGTON TRAVELLER,
div.p: CROOKING DEATH OF A WARRINGTON TRAVELLER,
WASHED OVERBOARD A MANX STEAMER.

A most painful sensation was caused in Warring- ton when it became known that the stormy passage of the Fenella, the Isle of Man Co.'s steamer from Liverpool to Douglas had resulted in the loss of three lives and one of them that of a well-known Warrington man. An exhaustive inquiry has been held by the directors of the Isle of Man Steam Packet Company, which only confirms the worst fears that the following gentlemen were washed overboard during the storm : James Frederick White, 26, traveller for the Mer- sey Bedstead Manufacturing Compeny, Warring- ton.

William Quayle, aged about 40, schoolmaster, Liverpool, and himseli a Manxman ; and John Scarratt, about 40, traveller for Hodgson and Sewell, bedstead manufacturers Birmingham. Quayle and Scarratt were seen off by relatives at the Landing-stage, and theluggage belonging t 3 all three was found on the vessel. Theirs was the only unclaimed passengers' luggage there was, though it was rumoured in Douglas on Sunday that arother man was lost, a traveller named Thomas. represent- ing a Leeds firm. This strry is discredited by the ateampacket,officials, and nothing is known to the police. It appears from an interview which a cor- respondent has had with a passenger named John 31cCoombe, that he was in all probability, in the company of the missing men. He states that four gentlemen besides himself an I a young lady were seated inside the open deck shelter in the front of the saloon, and a fifth gentleman was hold- ing on to the side partition when a big wave swept the vessel and threw them and the shelter on to the deck, probably ten feet away. He was picked up in a semi-unconscious state by some passengers who were standing in the staircase leading to the saloon. The young lady was helped below bleeding profusely, and also one of the other gentlemen pas- sengers. Mr. MiCoombe asked alter the other occu- pants of the shelter some time later, but never saw them in the saloon. It was daylight at the time. The gentleman clinging to the shelter was tall and about 40, and wore a long topcoat and blue trousers. A middle-aged gentleman inside the seat bad a heavy dark moustache, and wore a check travelling cap with laps for the ears, and two of the other occupants were young men of from 25 to SO. They spoke very tittle, all being more or less seasick. It was quite possible for them to have gone overboard. Another passenger, Mr. Carnell,of Castletown, stated there was nothing before the • particular wave came to justify the passengers be- ing ordered below. It is over 40 years since a simi- lar fatality occurred on the Manx boat, the victim on that occasion being a lady. On Friday afternoon last a party of commercial travellers staying at Douglas began to feel anxious about their comrade Mr. White, and inquiries were Set on foot. The fact then became known that he bad been on board the Fenella and he bad never been heard of since her arrival in Douglas. Inquiries made in Warrington on Saturday have only confirmed the sad news. On Tuesday, Mr. A. Clay, a Warrington traveller, crossed to Douglas and telegraphed to ask whether Mr. White had gone over on Monday. The information was telegraphed back that he had. Mr. Clay thereupon made inquiries, and identified Mr. White's luggage at the Packet Company's offices. He communicated the result to Warrington. In the meantime the Chief Constable of Warrington had received a message from the Superintendent of .Police at Douglas expressing the fear that Mr. White had been washed overboard and drowned while crossing on Monday. 31r. White, who lived in Manchester-road, had been in the employ of the Mersey Bedstead Corcpany about three and a half years, and had been on busi- ness to the Isle of Man for them on many occa- mons. Be was about 26 years of age. The saddest feature of the affair is that he had been married only six months,having Married the daughter of Mr. Stephen Dale, builder,of Warrington. Deceased was a young man of great promise, and was,very highly thought of by his employers, The confirmation of the painful news has been received with widespread regret in Warrington, where he was well known. The deceased had been for a long time a prominent 311GMber ot the Young Men's Christian Association, and was secretary of the Padgate Wesleyan Sunday school. He received his early training in the office Of Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, Horsemarket-street,where be remained for about six years. He subsequently entered the /service of Mr. Westgartb, with whom be remained until he was appointed traveller for the Mersey Bedstead Company in Knutsford-road. On Thursaay week, the annual meeting in con- nection' with the Padgate Wesleyan Sunday School, was held. Mr. White had prepared a re- Port to read at this meeting, although it appears he feared there was a probability that he might not be present, and he accordingly told his Wife that if he did not get back in time she must ask the librarian, Mr. Ernest Andrews to read it. The deceased was re-elected secretary at the meet- ing. The concluding words of the report by the deceased show that he intended to renew his exer- tions in the interests of We school :—" The school is in an efficient state and we trust that the year on which we are now entering will be one of increased blessing, and that the labour of the teache.rs Sun- day by Sunday may have its reward in bringing the scholars to tho Saviour and leading men in early life to consecrate tberes4ves to His service"______

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
POLICE CASES.

At the Town Hall, Ndwton,on Saturday morning, Sarah Atherton, of Wigan, was charged before Mr. Gillespie with ;soliciting in Earlestown on Friday night. P.C. Benson sustained the charge and she was sent t 3 gaol for 14 days.

div.head: P.S.A.
div.p: P.S.A.

There was a fair attendance at the usual meeting of the P.S.A. on Sunday afternoon. Mr. 0. France presided, and a stirring address was given by Mr. J. Gooding. Vocal selections were given by Miss Hughes and recitations by Miss Newman. Mr. S. Dring presidea at the piano.

div.head: 1.0.G.T. HOPA OF EARLESTOWN LODGE.
div.p: 1.0.G.T. HOPA OF EARLESTOWN LODGE.

The usual meeting was held on Monday night presided over by Bro T. Cu.ler, C.T. There was a good gathering of membErs awl friends. One can- didate was admitted. The digest of the No, 1 Con- vention which is to be held at Atherton on Satur- day next was read. Bro T Cutler gave a vary favour- able report of the annual social, thanks being ten- dered to all the committee. The programme for the evening was in the hands of Bro Stanley. Songs and musical selections were nicely rendered. Arrangements were made for the reception of the Gleam of Sunshine L3dge, Traatnere, on Monday next.

div.head: WARGRA.VE CHURCH.
div.p: WARGRA.VE CHURCH.

On Sunday special sermons were preached in the above church by the Rev. J. A. McDonald, 11.11. chaplain to the troops in India. In the afternoon he gave a missionary address to the children. He stated he had spent n years in India and referred to the worth ano lasting work which the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, and the Church Missionary Society were doing in India. Mission- ary work, however, he said should not be calculated by numbers. The societies named did a noble work during the Indian famine which created tremend- One distress in our great dependency. At each ser- vice an appeal for funds in aid of foreign missions was made.
ALA.RMING INCIDEXT AT THE CO-OPERATIVE HALL

On Sunday an incident of an alarming nature which might very well have been attended with serious results, happened at the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown. The P.S.A. was being held, and dr. 0. France officiated as chairman whilst Mr. J.Good- ing was the principal speaker. Suddenly without the slightest warning, a large iron rose which sur- rounds a gasalier suspended from the ceiling gave way, and striking Mr. France on the side of the head and shoulder fell with a crash to the floor. There was much excitement, and several people, fearing Mr. France was seriously injured, left the hail. Mr. Gooding begged the people to keep calm, and Mr.Dring gave out a hymn. It was afterwards found that Mr. France was net seriously injured, but he had had a moEt marvellous escape.

div.head: NEWION CONGREGA.TIOSAL MUTUAL SOCIETY.
div.p: NEWION CONGREGA.TIOSAL MUTUAL SOCIETY.

In connection with this society a social was held on Monday evening instead of the usual meeting. The Rev. James 'Allatt presided, and opened the proceedings by an address in which he reviewed the work of the session so far as it had progressed. There were about 130 people present, and a very pleasant evening was spent. A capital programme was provided, and efficiently submitted, the follow- ing being the items :—Qaartette, " Let the hills re- sound ;" recitation, Mr Robinson ; song, "The flight of ages," Mr S Henderson; selections on the grap ao• phone; recitation, " The light brigade," Mr It A Duncan; song, Miss Mather ; song, "The trov3r," Nlr H H Law ; recitation, Mr ROinson ; auartette, "The belfry tower ;" recitation, Mr R A Duncan. An interesting address was given by Mc Vir Speak- man, and during the evening refreshments were handed round to those present. D MATH OF Miss. THACKER, EVILICSTOWN.

It will b 3 seen from an announcement in another column, that Mrs. Thacker of Cross-lane,Earlestown passed away on Monday at the age of 61 years, at the residence of her daughter Princes Park, Liver• pool. The deceased lady jut before the end of last year went to Manchester on business, and whilst there she caught a chill. She however did not think much of it, and her son-in-law coming to see her, she returned with him to Liverpool to spend the New Year holidays. Whilst there, pneumonia supervened and although medical aid was sum- moned, she succumbed to the disease on Monday. As a teacher of music Mr 4. Thacker was exception- ally well-known in this district and St. Helens where she formerly resided, and during her career she has tutored most of the best families in the neighbourhood, including the Gambles, Pilkingtons and McCorquodales. She was a sister of the em'neut musician Str John Stainer, one time organist of St,. Paul's Cathedral, now Examiner at all the training colleges in England and a successful composer of Church music. The funeral took place on Thurs- day at St. Helens, the Rev. T. R. Matthews officiat- ing.

div.head: POLICE COURT MISSION WORK.
div.p: POLICE COURT MISSION WORK.

A little more than two years ago the Diocesan Ex- ecutive of the Church of England Temperanci Society appointed an agent in connection with its Police Court and Prison Gate Mission to visit the local police courts. The results from his work at the courts and in the town and neighbourhood have been so beneficial that it has been considered desirable to aff3rd additional facilities for the further development of the work. A plot of land has been secured by the Diocesan EX9CU- tire off Wallgate, Wigsn, and an iron building has been erectid. Temperance meetings will be held .and a reading room where light refreshments may be ohtained, &c. It will be known as the Wigan Church of England Temperance Institute. The opening ceremony will be performed by the Lord Bishop of the diocese, on the afternoon of Saturday, the 14th inst. Ms lordship will be sup- ported by the Ven. Archdeacon Madden ; the Rev 11 C Bull, Rural Dean ; Rev R G Vatthevv, Rector; The Rev J Hirst, Diocesan Sicretary ; the Rev R Sebbs. Vicar of St. Thomas' &c. Mr James C Ockersly, J.P. will preside. This will be follow2d by a public tea. In the evening a public meeting will be held under the presidency of Dr Stuart, J.P.,when the speakers will be the Revs Canon Blundell, and R nostance, Vice-president and Chairman respectively of the Diocesan Branch, and Mr C W Harris the local missionary.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
PAINFUL ACCIDENT AT A Sr. HELENS GLASSV73RICS.

Ralph Kay, aged thirty-four, of 21., Brook-street, St. Helens, met with very serious injarieS on Monday,when employed at the British Plate Gtassvrrks, Ravenhead, St. Helens. It is stated that Kiy is a glassmaker. Soon after ten o'clock that night while Bay was in a stooping position fixing a rivet in a glass polishing, disc a heavy plate of glass that was being moved fell on his back. Fortunate'y he was not cut, but the g'ais was so heavy that it crushed the lower part of Say's body, and in- flicted se-ioul internal injuries. Dr. Masson was sent for, and the poor man was removed in an agonised and critical condition to the St. Helens Hospital.

div.head: ST. HELENS CONGREGATIONAL PASTORATE.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS CONGREGATIONAL PASTORATE.

The Rev. F. W. Clarke, 8.A.., who has been pastor of the Zion Chapel. Frome, Smserset, for twenty-three years, cemmeoced his mhaistry as pastor of the Congre- gational Church, St. Helens, on Sunday. Prior to the morning servics a special prayer meeting was held in the schools. clnductel by Mr. Clarke, which was well. at'ended. There was a good attendance at the chapel in the morning, when th 9 rev. gentleman prsached for the first time as minister of the church. He took for his text the words For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the bold;: and ourselves your servants for His sake" (11. Car. iv., 5). He gave a most earnest address on the service of Christ. and said it was en, of his chief duties not to preach great sermons, but the truth. He would endeavour to help and guide all those connected with that church.—ln ths evening the le 7 gentleman preached from the words. "Immanuel: Go.l is with us"(lsaiah vii.,l4),which he said he had selected as the motto for the year. EXTRAORDINARY SUDDEN DEATH. . . _

George Clare. aged twentv-fiye,-a-g-la-sinder, living at 68. Oldfield-street, St. Helens, was found dead in a back passage off Bolton-atreet, Parr, about live minutes to twelve on Saturday night. Clare was employed at Messrs Pilkington's Plate-glastl Works, and was the son of the late Mr George Clare, who was the licenses of the Union Vaults in Oldfield-street..He was a man of robust heaPh, and left the Griffin Inn.m College-street, kept by his bro`hrr. on Saturday night. He then went to the People's Palace. and was seen after the performance with two women. James Langton, of 16, Bolton-street heard a noise in the back passage, 'and went out and found deceased. Constable Fairhurst was called, and found that the man was quite dead. Mr Coroner Brighouse held an inquest at St. Helens Town Hall on Tuesday on the body of George Clare. After hearing the evidence that of Dr. Knowles showing that death resulted from syncape, probably due to an overloaded stomach and over-excitement acting on a weak heart—the jury re- turned a verdict of" Death from natural causes."—A woman of loose character named Slater, who was in the company of deceased at the time of his death, was severely rebuked by the coroner, who declared his belief that she had told a lie on oath.

div.head: NEWTON DIVISION VACANCY,
div.p: THE NEWTON DIVISION VACANCY,

On Saturchr afternoon the Committee appointe 1 by the Liberal 300 on the previous Saturday to select a candidate to contest the vacancy in the Liberal interest, trit in the Co-operativa Hall under till presidency of Mr. G. W. Riwlins.

The meeting was private, but at the close, Mr. R tw- lins informed the reporters who were wilting, that the meeting had decided, that as no suitable candidate could be found, the present eleztion would not be con- tested.
The writ wal received at Preston on Tuesday, and the day for receivine nominations has been fixed for the 1611 inst. at the Town Hall, Newton. COLONEL PILKINGTON AT WARRINGTON.

On Wednesday afternoon Colonel PILKINGTON ad- dressed a meeting of electors in the Warringtoe Polling District, in the Assembly-room at the C3nservative Club, Warrington. In the absence of Alderman it W Fran- comb, the chair was occupied by Alderman Sutton, who was supported by Alderman Hutchinson, Messrs A Jolley, E C Ceoper, A Bennett, G Pilling, J Smethurst, R B Matthews, A Warburton, J Benne% A Daniels, Peter Naylor, J Branwood, James McCullum, C Reiland, 1G Jolley, H Hoult, A H Mather, G M Weer, Holland I ()wen (electio I agent) and Dr. Cannel'. The CHAIRMAN in opening his remarks, said consider- ing Colonel Pilkiegten'a ability, experience, and popu- larity, they could not be surprised that no opponent had yet had the courage to contest the seat with him. (Applause.) Colonel PILICINGTON, in the course of an address, said that when the present Government came into office three and a half years ago it was a curious thing that storms seemed to arise from almost every point. More diffi- culties arose than was the case during the three years the Liberals were in power, or in the previous adminis- tration of Lord Salisbury. The difficulties which had to Ibe faced were something very great. There were several I first rata difficulties. One of the greatest was the diffi- culty with America abeut Venezuela. Their thanks were due to Lord Salisbury for the careful, calm, and cool way with which be dealt with that very critical position.—(Cheers.) It would have Wen a vary serious thing, and one mach to be deplored, if they had been drawn into war with their relations in the United States. (Hear, hear.) That position had now been replaced by a cordial feeling between the two countries which no- body would have expected twenty years ago. They were probably aware of the kind of thing which was written about England in America for a nu.nber of years and if anyone had prophesied that the present state of things would exist so soon very few would have believed it possible. It was the work of Lord Salisbury and his Government.—(Cheers.) They knew very well that the crowning act of that splendid piece of work was the handling of the position when the United States was at war with Spain. It was thought of, andsuggested,that the European Powers should compel America to do err Cain things, but England would not have it, and it was pointed out at once, that instead of b Ana on the side of the great Continental nations we shou'd be on the side of our relations and people of our own blood across the water. We said in effect to the Continental nations "If you are going to bully them, you will find us on their side. That is all." (Laughter and cheers.) That was the crowning finish on the part of Lord Salisbury which had made the present position of friendliness and affection with our blood relations across the sea. (Hear, hear.) The speaker proceeded to speak of the Transvaal difficulty, which, he said, was a severe thing while it lasted. They were all sorry that the German Emperor sent the telegram he did. He believed the German Emperor was improving. He was not altagether the man in a hurry that he was a few years ago. (Laugh- tn..) He certainly was a man in a hurry when he sent that telegram. When they wrote a telegram in a hurry they were liable to say something that they did not mean. When the telegram was made known the wholel nation sprang up as if stung by ale insult. He did net think the Emperor meant to insult us, bat he ought notl to have interfered. If they went between a man and I his wife when there was a quarrel they would make a great mistake. (Laughter.) The Emperor came be- tween the Transvaal and ourselves when they were both pretty hot—(laughter)---and anyone coming in at that time was sure to catch it, and he caught it. (Laughter.) The difficuly showed us to be a brave and united nation that was not going to be insulted, and also that we had a force that could be mobilised at once. (Hear, bear.) A great deal had been said about Lord Salisbury's hesi- tancy and indecision but the proof of the pudding was in the eating, and when they looked at each one of these foreign questions' first at its • position three and a half ' years ago and then at its position to-day, they would find that Lord Salisbury and his Gavernmeat had been well acquained with the facts, had coolly dealt with them, and bad been equal to dealing with the crises when they arose. (Applause.) Ever since 1.888 they had been arming the nation as it ought to be armed, giving their attention first to the navy, which wan our traditional bulwark against f *reign foss and the trad.- Mona! bond between ourselves and our dependenees and colonies beyond the seas. (Hear, hear.) They had also: done their best to strengthen the Army, and they were I still continuing that policy. (Applause.) With regard to our nresent difficulties, Lord Crotner made a speech' at Khartoum the other day which revealed what was t I be our future policy in E gyot aed the Soudan. For I some years now our policy there had been a se Mel one, but previously there had been a great amount of inde- cision, which had formed a difficulty in the way of Lord Salisbury. The Soudan was now under the English and Egyptian flags, and Lord Kitchener had gone there alone, no doubt under Lord Cromer, and subject to the I Crown, to administer its affairs. Lord Salisbury had shown distinstly that he had a settled pelicy,and it was quite time it was settled. (Hear, hear.) As a result of this firm adm'nistration, we had cal:ten-el what he hoped would prove a permanent friendship with America. Our Colonies were enthusiastically British, and the position of the British Empire was stronger than it had ever been since the days of Waterloo. (App'ause.) In these cireUmstatnes, they could not be surprised that he was an enthusiastic and loyal sipposter of Lord Salisbury. (Applause.) Mr. GEORGH PILLING moved a resolution pledging sup- port to Colsnel Pilkington in the event of a contest. Mr. A. BENNETT, in seconding, said the candidate had given evidence of his spirit of independence and fidelity to his prineiples by joining the Unionist party upon the advent of Home Rule. (Applause.) It was significant that the more he had seen of Conservatism the more convinced bad he become that it represented the sound- est and wisest policy. (Hear, hear.) His experience of Conservatism had, in fact, made him an out and out Conservative. (Applause). In his (the speaker's) opinion, Conservatism which had been to Some extent permeated by Liberal Unionism represented the ideal party, and commended itself to the vast majority of the people of this country. (Aprlause.) Mr. GEORGE MATHER and Mr. R. B. MATTHEWS sup- ported. Mr. MATTHEWS said he trusted Colonel Pilkington would use any power he might have in the House of Commons to which he was now practically elected, to reduce the evil effects that might accrue through the recent Vaccination Act. They had felt the effect of the compulsory vaccination &awes that had been exercised for 50 many years with very great benefit to the whole community. He would like to have an assurance that if possibte a certain amount of compulsory vaccination should be enforced. The conscientious clause bad been exercised in no fewer than 275,000 cases of children. Fortunately it had not affected that district mach, but still it was a alig'st blot that might be removed and if possible done away with. Colonel PILICINGTON said with reference to the re- marks of Mr. Matthews he should forget what had been said, and the matter should recsive his careful ateen- tion. _ _
Th. ;meting concluded with the passing of a vote of thank; to the Chairman on tie propolition of C)Ionel PILRINGTON, seconded by Clumillor SMETHURST.
