div.head: STREET ACCIDENT.
div.p: STREET ACCIDENT.

Shortly after eleven o'clock on Saturday morning a serious accident happened opposite the Park, in t!ankey-street. A number of boys were running be- hind a lurry when one of their number,a boy named John Norman, ten years of age, living at 4, Glass- house-row, ran out towards the footpath and was knocked down by a passing bus and run over. He sustained severe injuries to his thigh,and was taken to the Infirmary. _ _

div.head: AUXILIARY OFFICERS' EXAMINATION
div.p: THE AUXILIARY OFFICERS' EXAMINATION

On Saturday,it was anuoum:ed that the following Warrington officers passed at the examination held in November :—Major J. D. Buckton and Captain J. A. Elelsten (distinguished), Ist V.B. South Lan- cashire. in organisation and equipment; Ciptains B. Fairclough and J. D. Fairclough, and Lieutenants G. R. Crusfield and E. E. Bernhard, Ist V. 13. South Lancashire, in tactics. COLLISION WITH A RUNAWAY H.ORSH AT WARRINGTON.

On Wednesday night,about 6.15, a horse attached to a cab owned by Mr. Arthur Wiison,Friars'-green, was left standing outside the Saracen's Head, Wil- derspool, when it bolted, and proceeded at a terrific rate towards Warrington. It want over Warrington Bridge and proceeded up to Market Gate, where it c )11ided with a bread van. P.C. Healey, wdo was on duty at Market-gate, caught the shafts of the vehicle and worked his way to the horse's head, and, with the assistance of P.S. Evans, brought the animal to a standstill down Horsemarket-street. Fortunately, no one was hurt,but the springs of the cab were damaged.

div.head: CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCHOOL.
div.p: THE CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCHOOL.

There was an important meeting on Monday of subscribers to this institution to consider a proposal that the children of laymen should be admitted. The Dean of Manchester (Canon Maclure) presided over a large attendance,. The school was established 50 years ago, expressly and solely for tne daughters of clergymen in the Liverpool, Chester, and (part of the) Manchester dioceses. It can acc)mm3date about 61 scholars, and tte number at present being educitel there is 58, The proposil to admit the children of laymen was made with a view to clearing off the debt of £BOO resting on the institu- tion, but at Monday'a meeting, after a long discus- sion, it was chcided to make no alteration in the existing arrangements. ST. ALBANS SCHOOLS.—ANNUAL S9IREB.

Oa Tuesday evening a successful soiree was held in Parr Hall, the proceeds being devoted to St. Albau's schools. The affair is ati annual one, and was held under the patronage of the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Wright). Complete arrangements had been made by a committee of gentlemen connected with St. Alban's Roman Catholic Church. Lie hall and corridors bad been charmingly decorated by Messrs. Hesketh and Dutton, and presented a very pleasing appearance. A number of slants lent to the committee were effectively utilized in the decoration of the building:. Dancing commenced at eight o'clock, and was con- tinued until half oast two in the morning. There were about 200 present. The M C's were Messrs. T. Knowles and W Brooks. The dance music was sup- plied by Mr. Percy Randall's band. The ladies of the congregation and others provided the refresh- ments. and the bar was in the capable charge of Mrs. Brown, of t'le Old Coffee House, MEETINGS OF SPIRITUALISTS.

The children of the Lyceum assembled in the Academy-street Temperance Hall on Saturday even- ing, and sat down to a tea provided by the ladies connected with the institution out of funds specially subscribed for that purpose. The tables and the rostrum were nicely decorated with vases of flowers and two small Christmas trees, and the room pre- sented a very cheerful appearance. After tea the room was cleared, and an entertainment was given by some of the children and adults, and consisted of recitations. solos, duets and trios, and the children also went through their manhing and calisthenic exercises. This was followed by games, in which those who entered enjoyed themselves thoroughly, and on leaving each was presentei with an orange. —On Sunday and Monday, Mrs. Hulme, of Man- chester, fulfilled her first engagement with this society, and was greeted with good audiences. The subjects of her Sunday addresses were' Never alone" and "The phenomena and philosophy of Spiritualism." After each address, as also on the Monday evening, Mrs. Hulme gave a number of psychometric delineations.
kiNCEIESTER AND LIVERPOOL DISTRICT BANKING
COMPANY, LIMITED.

The meeting of tte shareholders of this banking company will be held at the head office, Spring Gardens, Manchester, on Wednesday next at twelve o'clock noon, to receive the report of the directors, and the balance sheet of the company, as at 31st December last, to declare a dividend and elect direc- tors. In their report the directors state that the gross profit for the half year ending 31st December last, after providing for all bad and doubtful debts is £195,9i9 17s 3d to which has to be added the amount brought forward from 30th June lait amounting to £22,892 33 81., making a total of £218,802 03 11d. From this sum the following de- ductions have to be made :—Total expenßes at the head office, the London office and branches including salaries, stationery. taxes, &c., £73,883 14s 83, in- come tax £6,473 178 Od, leaving a net profit of £138,441 98 31. The directors recommend the declaration of a dividend of 15s a share and a bonus of 5s a share, which will take £lOO,OOO, leaving a balance of £33,444 94 33. Of this it is proposed to carry to the reserve fund £l5 000 and to next account £23,441 9s 3d. The directors whose terms of office expires on the 18th inst are Messrs. George Barbour, Abel Buckley, Frank Gemmill Crowther, Edward Donner, and James Halliday. They are eligible and recommended for re-election. LOYAL PRINCE OF WALES LODGE.

The annual meeting of the above Oddfellows Lodge was held last week at the Pelican Hotel, But- termarket-street. The Noble Grand, Mr. A Ratcliffe, preside,ci. There was a large number of members present. The accounts were presented by the Secretary which showed that the receipts during the past year amounted to £629 is 611, and the ex- penditure in sick pay &c., £515 Os Bid. showing a saving during the year of £ll4 03 10S. After dis- cussion on the accounts which several members took part in, a resolution was passed confirming their adoption and that £5O be tran4lerred from the Management Fund, and £2O from the Benevolent Fund to the credit of the Sick Fund. The total worth of the Lodge now amounts to £2055. There has been an increase of 14 members during the year. The Ledge n ree consists of 335 members and the average age is 33 years and 8 months. Vice- Grand J. L. Peers was installed Noble Grant for the coming year, and a hearty vote of thank 3 was re- corded to the retiring officers, and all present seemed pleased to know the Lodge had had such a successful year in 1893, and also that progress had been so steady for years past. The best thanks of the meeting were given Mr. Ratcliffe for presiding and the meeting then closed in ordinary form.
LECTURE AT THE CHRISTADELPHIIN ROOM.

Mr. B. Lake,or Stockpon,lectured in the Christa- delphian room, Blld-street, on Sunday evening, his subject being "A Bible fact, coming destruction of the Papacy :—A Divine retribution." The lecturer remarked that the reason of his coming before them was that it was a Bible fact that the Papacy was to be destroyed, notwithstanding the revival of Rornanism in England, and the advance of Ritual- ism in the Church of England, come particulars of which were given. There was not much difference between Protestants and Catholics, for they both believed in three Gods in one, which was not in the Bible, and that human beings had immortal souls which went to heaven or hell at death,the Catholics having a special middle place—purgatory—where the souls remained a length of time varying with the length of a man's puree. Generally speaking I the Protestants had fought for civil and religion liberty, while the motto of the Romanists was "The end justiffes the means,' and though the sword had gone rusty in the scabbard if Roman Catholics were in the ascendency it would be soon furbished again. Mr. Lake, after observing that the Protestants had protested against the cruder doctrines of Rome only, proceeded to scripturally prove the identity of Paul's "Man of sin," "Mystery of iniquity," and John's "Babylon and mother of harlots," with the Papacy, which would be destroyed when Christ returned to the eartk again. Nearly all students of prophecy were agreed that we were fast nearing the time of Christ's return to the earth again, and he earnestly asked them to carefully consider what had been brought to their no' ice, accepting what was in accord with the Bible, for he did not wish them to accept anything unless it was strictly in accord- anca with the scripture proof adduced.

div.head: TREAT TO POOR CHILDREN
div.p: TREAT TO POOR CHILDREN
AT WARRINCiTON.
CHRISTMAS TREE AND ENTERTAIN- MENT IN PARR HALL,

On Wednesday evening the long expected treat to the poor children of the town oE Warrington was brought off in happy manner and generous style. The treat was not exactly limited to the children however, for the keen pleasure experienced by the crowd of spectators WhO thronged tha gallery of Parr Hall, and the ladies and gentlemen who threw themselves into the work of providing one night of unalloyed pleasure to those whose lot is so hard,was apparent to the most casual observer. There were probably twelve hundred little ones, both boys and girls, with clean faces full of expectancy, seated in the large hall, and happy in each others company, That sight alone was ample recompense to those who have worked so devotedly and unselfishly for the benefit of the youngsters. It is unneces,ary to say that the children required no pressing when the repast commenced, and they devoted themselves to consuming the milk, buns, and other good things with hearty appe- tites, no doubt in many cases keenly sharpened by actual want. They were waited on by the attendants most assiduously. While the children regaled themselves Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., played suitable volun- taries on the organ. When the material wants of the children had been sa'isfie I to the full, preparations were made for the comnsencement of the entertainment, the details of which showed that the most careful thought had been brought to boar upon this pie:, of the treat. All the items were caleulated to suit the infantile minds of the audience' aad afford them pleasant contrast to their daily life and surroundings. The horseshos shape of the gallery had been decor- ated with suspended chines(' lanterns and the front of the stage was festooned with the array of presents of all descriptions, flanked on either side by two huge Christ- mas trees, their branches bending beneath the weight of presents, which almost hid leaf and branch. The rear of the stage was completely taken up by a large number of prettily dreise I children and young ladies, many of whom were attired in character costumes. Tne whole arrangement made up a scene calcula- ted to put everybody in a most cheerful frame of mind. Tne Mayor was unfortunately unable to be present owing to a business engagement at London in connection with the Corperation,and in a letter to Mr. W.H.J.Jenkins(hen. treas. )which wag read by the latter, exprered his perfect sympathy with the entertain- ment. The Mayoress, Mr. Jenkins, Mr. H. Taylor (hon. sec.), the members of the committee, and other ladies and gentlemen were iudefstgible in their endeavours to secure tjoe complete enjoyment of the youngsters. A little sketch in which were Father Christmas, and Old Mother Time in excellent character costrimes,introduced the preccedings. Toe advent of the Punch and Judy show, however, was hailed with extreme delight, the family troubles and laughable doings of the famous couple bong followed with sympathetic interest. A floral (Janne b 7 young ladies, the pupils of the Misses Reynolds, was most gracefully executed. Mr. Grounds eont,ributed some ventriloquism and hie gramophene entertainment prevrel an agreeable surprise to his young audience. Anetlier dance by two pupils of Vie Missei Reynolds, in chiracter costumes representing Pierot and Pierette was appreciated most heartily, the abilities of the young ladies being unquestionable. Mr. Beale's comic songs proved most agreeable items. But it was reserved for the com'c lantern slides by Mr. T)--'or to score the suc- cess of the evening. They were received with enthus- iastic aeplause and when finally the photoeraples of the Mayor and Mayoress were thrown upon the screen, the ball wee filled with deafening cheers and the portraits were called for again and again. When the entertain- ment was concluded, the children were marched on to the platform in an orderly manner, and the Mayoress then presented etch one with a Ceris'm es present, and they departed home, their cup of enjeyinent filled to the brim, and with the memory of one happy day, at least, to look back upon with cont( fitment.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

THURSDAY. —'-Before his Honour Jevige Ffoulkes. CLAIM FOR RENT.—Thomas Unsworth, buteher, Lumb Brook, Grappenhall, sued James Richardson, painter. Sandy- lane, Orford, for rent due.—Mr. Willett represented the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Browne, the defendant. —Mr. Willett said the plaintiff's claim was for £4 155., the rent of a house in Orford-lane, in which the defendant ha .1 lived for 15 months up to May last. A fortnight after qnarter day be wished to give notice to expire with the current quarter. Plaintiff refused to accept the notice, but a short time after- wards defendant's wife saw him and he told her he would accept it. Thinking defendant was leaving the house he ad- vertised it to be let on the 17th Angust. A day or two after this the defendant's wife again saw plaintiff, and said they could not leave owing to some pigs they had on the prcmises. On the 17th August a letter was written by the defendant in which h: said be gave three months' no`ice to leave the house on the 17th November, 1893, and adding that the house" was not properly speaking habit- able during the winter, and that it was dear enough if one had to pay only the rates and not the £l9 rent." The plain- tiff was ert;.aged at the Norton Arms Hotel when the defend- ant's wife went to him and said she had come to give up the keys. He refused to take them, and a short time after a boy came and put the keys on a table. The plaintiff swept them off and refused to take thern.—After evidence by the plaintiff Mr. Browne said his client gave notice a fortnight too late. —His Honour : There is no getting beyond the defendant's letter —Mr Browne : I hope to satisfy you that it was done , away with.—Mr. 13rowne said his case was that his client gave the wrong noqee. but when he saw the advertisement he assumed that Mr Unsworth was accepting the invalid notic . He sent his wife to ask to be permitted to stop loner. She did not know the contents of the letter of her husband, and he (Mr Browne) contended that the arrange- ment made with Mr Unsworth did away with the letter.— His Honour : I cannot accept that, although it is very in- genious on the part of yOur client. A letter *as sent giving notice to quit on the 17th November. The notice is binding on your client, and he must pay the rent. There will be a verdict for plaintiff for the amount of the claim, to be paid at the rate of £1 a month. DispuTß RESPECTING THE PURCHASE oP A HORSE.— Edward Rawes, Crowley Hall. Arley, near Northwieh, sued Mrs Sudlow, contractor, Howley, for the value of a horse, £2s.—Mr. A Browne represented the plaintiff and Mr Long- ton, the defendant.—ln orening the case Mr. Browne stated that Mr. Rawes was a horse dealer, and he had an agent in Warrington named Mr James Cottam. Mrs. Sudlow was a carting contractor and had a number of horses. She engaged a number of stepsons to assist her in the business. At the beginning of October, Mr Cottam had three horses to sell, and knowing that Mrs. Sudlow wanted a horse, he sent Mrs. Cottam, his wife, to see Mrs Sudlow. Mrs Cottam did so, and some discussion took place. Mrs Cottam told her that the price was £25 which could be paid in two instalments, one on the Ist November. and the ether on the let December. It was decided that the horse should he cent for a week's trial, and Mrs. Cottam stated that her husband would come and complete the arrange- ments. The horse was sent on the Bth October and on the following day Mr. Oottam saw Mrs. Sudlow and she con- firmed the arrangement come to on the previous day,namely that the horse should be sent for a week's trial and that the price. £25 was to be paid in two instalments. Instead of having the horse on trial for a week, Mrs. Sudlow had kept it eight weeks. On the Ist of December Mrs. Sudlow told Mr. Cottam that if Alfred who was one of the step-Sons wanted to keep the horse it would be all right. Mr. Cottam Saw Alfred and he stated that they did not want to part with the horse. They kept it for eight weeks but refused to pay, for it and denied having bought it. Mr. Cottam communi- cated with Mr. Rawes, the owner, and who afterwards in- structed him (Mr. Browns.) to write to the defendant. The following day he received a letter from Mr. Longton on be- half of Mrs. Sudlow. stating that the horse had been returned and that no purchase had been made. Mr. Browne, continu- ing his statement said the defendant had had the horse shod two or three days and had been con- tinually working it. He contended that tha defendant had clearly taken possession of it and that they had decided to buy it —Edward Eames, Mrs Cottam and Mr Cottam gave evidence bearing out Mr. Browne's statement. It was not customary to allow a horse out on more than a week's trial —For the defence Mr. Langton urged that the defendant never botaght the herse. Three horses were sent to Mr. Cottam by Mr. Rawes, and as he was unable to find stabling accommodation for them, Mr. Cottam sent his wife to Mrs Sudlow to see if she would find accommodation for one, stating that she could use it for keeping it No arrange- ments were made for purchasing it. Mr. Longton asked his Honour to consider whether it was likely that if Mr. Cottam intended to sell the horse that he would send his wife to enter into negotiations. He submitted th:t accord- ing to the evidence she gave no terms for the purchase were agreed upon.—His Honour: But they were afterwards ratified by ..Ir. Cottam.—Mr. Longton (continuing), said his defence was that Mr. and Mrs. Cottam had been endeavouring to push this horse upon the defendant. Mrs. Sudlow never intended to buy it, and as soon as she heard that an attempt was being made to hold her responsible for the price of it she returned it. The transactions respect- ing the purchase of the horse were limited to negotiations.—Mrs. Sudlow was then called and denied that either Mr. or Mrs. Cottam made any arrangement with her for the purchase of the horse. The first time she heard of the price was when she received a lawyer's letter. The arrange- ment was that she was to have the horse for its keep until a purchaser was found.—Alfred Siddall stated that when Mr Cottam told him the price of the horse was £25 he replied that it was net worth the money. He denied the statement of Mr Cottam that he agreed to buy it.—His Honour said it was an unfortunate case. There was direct pelury on one side or the other. If people would hold them- selves in such abominable crime, they must bear the brunt of 't if the decision went against th:.m. He had decided to give judgement for the plaintiff for the amount claimed. SUDDEN DEATH IN A HAYDOCK COLLIERY.

Andrew Rowley, 50 years of age. of Penny-lane, Flay- dock, died suddenly in the Q,ieen Pit, Flaydock, owned by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., on Monday morning. He was working as a collicr when he suddenly fell for- ward and expired tefore he could be removed out of the colliery.

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A. HAYDOOK MAN. At the Warringto e Occasional Court on Monday, be- fore Mr. S. K. Armitage, John Griffiths, of Hayclock,was charged with unlawfully and indecently assaulting and illtreating Martha. Roberts on the 7th January. Com- plainant is the wife of Edward Roberts, of 5. Flaydock- lane,Havdock.collier and local preacher' and the prisonv had lodged with the Roberts' for about a raontb.—He was committed to the next Liverpool ;Sessions for trial. 111.- ATTEUPTED SUICIDE AT WARRINGTON. On Sunday, Ezra Dutton, 18 Warburton-street, was taken to the Warrington Infirmary suffering from the effect; of a mixture of ammonia and camphorated oil. It appears that be returned home on Saturday night un- der the influence of drink. In an early hour of the morning he seired a medicine bottle containing liniment, poured out a quantity into a basin and drank it. His mother-in-law and several friends found him lying on the floor uaconscions, and he was removed to the Infir- mary. It felrll9 that Dutton has suffered from lumbago and has been in a despondent state of mini for the last month. On Wednesday at the Borough Police Court, Ezra Dot. ton waa brought before Mr. James Fairclough (chair- man) and other magistrate; and charged with attempt- ing to commit suicide.—Tne Chief Constable repeated the fact; as stated above and added that the man worked at a glass works in St. Helens,and his employers had given him a very good characte% The liniment had been given him from the Infirmary for his back, as he had had pains both in his head and back for some tlme.—On the promise of his relatives to look after him the magis- trates withdrew the charze.
